It happened because for the past twelve years, the country has prioritised the welfare and empowerment of the poor. During these twelve years, the nation received a leak-proof system. Through DBT, every rupee sent from Delhi reached the poor. Free ration and free healthcare helped poor families save money. Crores of permanent houses, crores of toilets, and smoke-free kitchens made life easier for the poor. Crores of people received the protection of insurance, which became a source of support during times of crisis. Before 2014, even 25 crore people in the country did not have any social security coverage. Today, nearly 100 crore people in the country have been connected to a social security safety net.

Friends,

Today, when the entire nation is remembering and paying tribute to Sardar Saheb, his soul must surely be blessing us. Through such efforts, we will eliminate poverty from the country and build a Developed India.

Friends,

National unity guarantees a nation’s stability and success. And in times of global instability such as these, the importance of unity has increased even more. You all know that today the world is burning in the fires of unrest. This is among the most difficult periods of the past several decades. Wars are taking place between many countries around the world. Major economies are struggling with challenges. The crisis of resources continues to grow. Global supply chains are becoming fragmented. At such a time, India’s unity, the unity of all Indians, is our greatest strength. Because it is this unity that will help us overcome every storm.

Brothers and sisters,

In recent months, we have seen the world struggling with an energy crisis. In some countries, limits were even imposed on the purchase of petrol and diesel. It was being said that India would face the biggest crisis because it has such a large population and does not produce sufficient petroleum. Amid these concerns, anti-India forces also became active.

But friends,

This is India’s strength. We did not allow the impact of this global energy crisis to fall upon our citizens. This is certainly a diplomatic and strategic success for the country, but the unity and solidarity of our people played an equally important role. While the nation was looking for solutions to external challenges, certain forces within the country were busy spreading lies and rumours in an attempt to create instability. But the people of India stood shoulder to shoulder with the nation. This is the greatest strength of this country. This is the strongest foundation of our confidence.

Friends,

When great leaders such as Sardar Patel and Babasaheb Ambedkar created the Constitution of India, they established the system of a ruling side and an opposition side. They also explained the importance of this arrangement. In a democracy, the responsibility of the opposition is to oppose government policies. But unfortunately, in today’s India, the opposition has abandoned its duty and has transformed itself from an opposition into an obstruction. In its frustration and despair, it has begun placing obstacles in the path of the country’s development. This is not opposition; this is obstruction. They have made it the basis of their politics. They are engaged in tearing apart the dignity and spirit of the Constitution.

Friends,

These forces are continuously engaged in conspiracies to divide the nation. Attempts are being made to divide and pit against one another the children of Mother India. Due to more than a decade of frustration and disappointment, these people have now come out in the open. We must identify who is secretly meeting whom abroad, which anti-India forces are supporting whom, and who is speaking the language of India’s enemies. We must recognise these patterns. We must unite and confront them. Especially the way social media is being used as a weapon, the way rumours are being spread, and the efforts being made to damage India’s image, all citizens must come together to deal with these challenges. We have ended Naxalism in remote regions. But the threat of intellectual Naxalism has not yet disappeared from the country. The nation must always remain vigilant against these intellectual Naxals.

Friends,

No matter how difficult the circumstances may be, we must not allow this grand mission of national unity and this journey towards a strong and capable India to stop. We must now work towards the next major goals. We must secure the nation’s borders completely. We must stop infiltration and demographic changes caused by it. We must also move forward towards a Secular Civil Code.

Friends,

Whenever a nation takes great resolutions, whenever it takes major decisions, obstacles will arise, difficulties will appear, and storms will have to be faced. But India is no longer going to stop. The mantra of “Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat” and the goal of a Developed India have now become India’s unwavering resolve. We will push ourselves to the limits of hard work. We will confront every storm with determination. But our eyes will remain fixed on one objective alone: building a strong, capable, and developed India by 2047, when the nation completes 100 years of independence. This passion must be present in every effort we make and in every breath we take. This idea must beat with every heartbeat in our hearts. With this resolve, I once again extend my heartfelt greetings to all of you on National Unity Day.

Bharat Mata Ki Jai!

Bharat Mata Ki Jai!

Bharat Mata Ki Jai!

Vande Mataram.

Vande Mataram.

Vande Mataram.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-speech-at-the-launch-of-development-:
Bharat Mata Ki Jai.

Bharat Mata Ki Jai.

Popular Chief Minister of Gujarat Shri Bhupendra Bhai Patel, Deputy Chief Minister Bhai Harsh Sanghvi ji, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly Shri Shankarbhai Chaudhary, all ministers of the Gujarat Government, Members of Parliament and Members of the Legislative Assembly, other public representatives, brothers and sisters.

Today, through technology, farmers from every district of the country are connected with us. Today, through technology, farmers from every village of Gujarat are connected with us. Chief Ministers of different states, ministers, all of them are with us today in this important programme for farmers. I heartily welcome all of them as well.

Today, Banaskantha has established its stature. Just now, I was watching on the screen that perhaps such a large gathering seated on charpoys has never been held anywhere in the world. For the people of the country too, it must be an amazing sight that everyone in this gathering is seated on charpoys. Today, Banaskantha has revived this great tradition of our villages. Had you informed the Guinness Book of World Records in advance, they would certainly have recorded it as a world record. It was just mentioned here a moment ago.

The responsibility that you entrusted to me has now completed twenty-five years. And look at the coincidence, after completing twenty-five years, my first visit has been to our Banaskantha. Let me remind you that after becoming Chief Minister in 2001, my first major public programme as Chief Minister was held in Deesa. The older people here will remember that Lok Kalyan Mela. That programme was perhaps historic. Three lakh people from a single district attended it. I do not believe that record has been broken to this day. That record belongs to Banaskantha. The journey began there, and today I have got the opportunity to present an account of twenty-five years of service at the same place.

Only a few days after Navratri, I have received the opportunity to come to the sacred land of Mother Amba. I bow at the feet of Mother Amba. A short while ago, projects dedicated to women, children, farmers, and livestock rearers were inaugurated and foundation stones laid here. A new instalment of PM-Kisan Samman Nidhi has also reached the accounts of crores of small farmers across the country. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to the people of Gujarat, to the people of the country, and to farmers across India.

Friends,

The people of Gujarat and Banaskantha should forgive me, but I have to speak in Hindi today because people from all over the country are connected with this programme. You permit me to speak in Hindi, don’t you? Very good.

Friends,

Our farmers, our food providers, are among the strongest pillars of a Developed India. Our government has always prioritised the welfare and empowerment of farmers. Compared to 2013–14, the agricultural budget of the country has now increased more than five times. PM-Kisan Samman Nidhi has become a part of the lives of crores of small farmers. Today, more than ₹18,000 crore has been transferred into the accounts of nearly ten crore farmers. More than fifty lakh farmers of Gujarat have also benefited from it. More than ₹1,000 crore has been deposited into their accounts. In Banaskantha alone, nearly ₹50 crore has reached the accounts of lakhs of farming families.

Friends,

Because of our government’s policies over the past years, farmers have received benefits or savings worth more than ₹50 lakh crore. Fifty lakh crore rupees. Let me give you an example of just five schemes. Around ₹4.5 lakh crore under PM-Kisan Samman Nidhi has directly reached the bank accounts of small farmers. Sister, you have defeated me. I thought you would sit down after a while because your hands would start hurting. I request the SPG personnel to collect that beautiful picture which this daughter has brought. Otherwise, she will grow tired holding it up. They will collect it from here, my child. Please stay where you are. Let the SPG personnel collect it. After Independence, the needs of small farmers were never truly understood. Nobody paid attention to them. Yet small farmers account for more than 85 percent of all farmers in our country. More than 85 percent. It is our government that understood their concerns and supported them through PM-Kisan Samman Nidhi.

Friends,

Over the past few years, global uncertainties caused fertiliser prices to surge sharply. But a government dedicated to farmers did not allow that burden to fall upon them. The government spent nearly ₹16 lakh crore on this. To ensure that fertilisers remain affordable for you, we had to spend ₹16 lakh crore from the national treasury, so that the burden would not fall upon our farmers.

Friends,

Previous governments repeatedly misled farmers on Minimum Support Price. But ours is the government that fulfilled its MSP promise. Over the past twelve years, farmers growing wheat and paddy have received ₹24 lakh crore in MSP payments directly into their accounts.

Friends,

Our government has provided farmers with a powerful safety net through the PM Fasal Bima Yojana. We launched crop insurance on a large scale. During the past ten to twelve years, farmers have received more than ₹2 lakh crore in crop insurance compensation. Whenever crops suffered losses, over ₹2 lakh crore reached farmers through insurance support. We are continuously trying to reduce farmers’ irrigation costs as well. PM-KUSUM is playing an increasingly significant role in this effort. Under this scheme, nearly twelve lakh solar pumps have already been provided. Twelve lakh pumps powered by solar energy have been given to farmers for irrigation. Because of this, the need for electricity and diesel has reduced substantially. If these solar pumps had not been provided, farmers would have had to purchase more than 80 crore litres of diesel. That entire expense has been saved by lakhs of farmers. And besides that, additional electricity has also been generated. If viewed in one way, these five schemes and decisions alone have either directly benefited farmers or saved them the equivalent of ₹50 lakh crore. This is an enormous figure. These ₹50 lakh crore have increased farmers’ incomes and strengthened Indian agriculture.

Friends,

Agriculture is our tradition. Agriculture is our culture. Agriculture is our culture. During the past twelve years, our government has extensively integrated science and technology into farming. We have linked agriculture and animal husbandry with scientific methods. Soil Health Cards are an excellent example of this. Earlier, farmers found it difficult to determine what type of fertilizer their fields required and in what quantity. Soil Health Cards solved this problem. Today, more than 26 crore Soil Health Cards are in the hands of farmers. These have modernised farming practices.

Friends,

Changing weather patterns are a major challenge for farmers. Therefore, our effort is to continuously provide farmers with new seed varieties that are better suited to changing climatic conditions. Over the past years, around three thousand new seed varieties have been made available to farmers.

Friends,

Animal husbandry is an important part of our rural economy, and our sisters have a major role in it. During the past decade, we have strongly promoted the use of science and technology in animal husbandry and the dairy sector. When livestock breeds improve, milk production increases. As Shankarbhai was saying earlier, we want one cow to produce as much milk as four cows once did. If animals receive timely vaccination and treatment, losses due to disease are reduced. In other words, healthier animals mean higher incomes for our livestock-rearing brothers and sisters.

Friends,

You are all familiar with the National Gokul Mission. Through it, indigenous breeds are being preserved and scientific breeding is being promoted. The new research centre established in Banaskantha will further strengthen this mission. Indigenous cattle breeds such as Gir, Sahiwal, and Kankrej, and buffalo breeds such as Mehsana, Murrah, and Jaffarabadi, will be preserved here. At the same time, major work will be done to improve their quality. For the Kankrej breed, this is the first facility of its kind in the country. Consider a farmer who owns a high-quality cow that produces more milk and remains healthy at a lower cost. Naturally, that farmer would want future generations of that cow to retain those same qualities. Modern technologies such as IVF help achieve exactly that. They increase the likelihood that superior traits will pass on to future generations. The direct benefit of this goes to livestock rearers.

Friends,

Protecting livestock from disease is also one of our priorities. Foot-and-mouth disease affects both animal health and milk production. Therefore, we launched a nationwide free vaccination campaign. So far, nearly 150 crore vaccine doses have been administered to animals. The livestock of more than eight crore farmers have received free vaccinations. This has also reduced the financial burden on livestock rearers.

Friends,

The impact of these efforts is visible in milk production as well. In 2013–14, a cow or buffalo produced on average less than five litres of milk per day. This was the situation when you sent me to Delhi. Less than five litres a day. Today, the national average has increased to around eight litres per day. India’s growth rate in milk productivity is the fastest in the world. India ranks number one globally in milk production. The benefits have reached villages, and the incomes of farming families have increased.

Friends,

We want livestock rearers to earn not only from milk but also from dung. Infrastructure is being developed for producing biogas, bio-CNG, and organic fertilisers from dung and agricultural residues. Institutions like Banas Dairy have an important role in this. Today, foundation stones have also been laid for two bio-CNG plants. Our objective is clear: healthier livestock, higher milk production, and complete utilisation of dung. We are transforming animal husbandry into not merely a tradition but also a strong means of increasing farmers’ incomes and enriching villages. I was interacting with the women here earlier. They told me they supply milk worth ₹2 crore. Milk worth ₹2 crore. Then I asked them how much education they had received. They replied, “Four books,” and yet they supply milk worth ₹2 crore.

Friends,

Over the past years, we have worked with a holistic approach for the prosperity of villages. Just look at the fisheries sector and see how much it has expanded. You will be pleased to know that India’s seafood exports have more than doubled. Our fishermen go out to sea, catch fish and shrimp, and sell them. Today, this sector has made enormous progress, and demand across the world has risen sharply. Cooperation in the fisheries sector is also being promoted.

Friends,

There is another sector that has provided an additional source of income for our farmers. That sector is beekeeping. Over the past twelve years, honey production has doubled. I remember that when I came to Banaskantha, I urged all of you to bring about a Sweet Revolution, a Honey Revolution. Today Banaskantha is setting new records in honey production. When I was interacting with the women earlier, they told me they sell honey worth ₹35 lakh. You will be proud to know that India has become the world’s second-largest exporter of natural honey. In this Sweet Revolution, the contribution of our women’s self-help groups is also steadily increasing.

Friends,

A few days ago, on 7th October, I completed twenty-five years as head of government. It feels as though it happened only yesterday. Yes, it feels like yesterday itself, when I first took the oath on 7th October 2001. You all gave your Narendra Bhai immense affection and immense love.Today, I felt a little awkward here. Whatever is said in the rest of the country is one thing, but here Shankarbhai said, “Prime Minister Sahib, Prime Minister Sahib.” Tell me honestly, how will such an address go down my throat? Here, people habitually say, “Our Narendra Bhai has come.” Doesn’t it feel better to say that? What joy is there in saying “Prime Minister Sahib”? And when my brothers from Gujarat say “Our Narendra Bhai,” my heart overflows with emotion. More than affection, every Gujarati taught me something. They guided me towards the right path and inspired me. At that time, I knew nothing about government offices, government functioning, or files. A person from an ordinary family, whose generations had never even dreamed of becoming the head of a village, was entrusted by you with the responsibility of serving first Gujarat and then the nation. Earlier while speaking with the women, they asked me how ideas such as Jyotigram, bringing water, natural farming, and initiatives for livestock came to me. I told them that there was no special formula. You taught me everything, and I simply went and implemented it.

Friends,

I have always known only two things: service to the people is service to the nation, and the development of Gujarat leads to the development of India. Everything else, how to work and how to move forward, you taught me. Whatever I have been able to do for the nation belongs to all the citizens of India, and to all of you as well. For this, I will remain indebted to you for my entire life. Until my final breath, I will remain devoted to service. Service, service, and service to the people of the country and to all of you.

Friends,

The senior citizens present here will still remember the old days. Twenty-five years ago, when I used to come here, there were severe problems of electricity and water. Even then, I used to say that we must save electricity and water. Farmers would protest against me, saying, “Who is Modi to tell us to save water? He won’t even give us electricity.” I kept arguing with you, and eventually you accepted what I was saying. And today, just look at where we have come from and where we have reached. Those old problems now remain only in memories. Today, I will once again tell you the same thing: we must save water, and we must save electricity as well.

Friends,

The waters of the Narmada and modern technologies such as drip irrigation have transformed Banaskantha. They have changed both the face and the destiny of Banaskantha. Banaskantha’s potatoes are now world-famous. No one can come to a person from Banaskantha and say, “I will turn potatoes into gold,” because he will reply, “I am already doing that.” We have a cooperative brand like Banas Dairy here, which is expanding the cooperative movement to other parts of the country, including Kashi. I am especially grateful to Banas Dairy because even in my Kashi, people are benefiting from your experience and your service. Now, even the French fries potato processing plant has expanded its capacity. This will make it possible to purchase a larger quantity of potatoes. This is a major facility and support for potato farmers.

Friends,

A Cluster Development Programme is being implemented for farmers engaged in fruit and vegetable cultivation. Under this programme, twelve clusters have been approved today. These clusters are associated with fruits and vegetables such as tomatoes, potatoes, chillies, grapes, bananas, onions, oranges, pomegranates, and cocoa. Under this initiative, farmers will be supported in establishing new orchards and rejuvenating old ones. People will be trained and guided for the rejuvenation of older orchards, and subsidies will be provided for the entire project. The two clusters approved in North Gujarat will greatly benefit potato farmers of Banaskantha and Sabarkantha.

Friends,

Today, several other development projects related to Gujarat have also been inaugurated and launched. Gujarat has received two new railway services: the Ahmedabad–Varanasi Sabarmati Express and the Mehsana–Becharaji–Sabarmati MEMU train. Both are highly significant rail connectivity projects. In addition, the Ahmedabad Metro service is also being expanded. Today, the foundation stone has been laid for metro projects connecting GIFT City and the airport. The Ahmedabad–Mehsana Highway is now set to be expanded from four lanes to eight lanes.

Friends,

Today, more than 4,000 modern Anganwadis are also being inaugurated for the children of Gujarat. Nearly four lakh children and pregnant mothers will benefit from them.

Friends,

Every such effort is aimed at making India a developed nation. Today, every farmer, every young person, and every daughter and sister in the country is moving forward with the resolve of building a Developed India. But unfortunately, some people do not like this. Some people are unable to accept it. These are people who want to see the country in difficulty. They derive satisfaction from seeing the nation in trouble. Whenever challenges arise for the country, they feel happy.

Friends,

A recent example of this is the war taking place around Iran and the Gulf region. At a time when India is united in dealing with its consequences, these people were busy spreading rumours. Rumours were spread among farmers that fertilisers would not be available. Artificial queues were created and the atmosphere was disturbed. Women were frightened by being told that cooking gas would no longer be available, asking them how they would cook food and how their children would go to school. Their plan was to create panic and disorder in the country so that they could defame Modi.

Friends,

I want to remind the farmer brothers and sisters of this country that I had said Modi would stand firmly with you. And you can see that even though the war is still continuing, Modi did not allow any shortage of fertilisers for farmers. We did not allow fertiliser supplies to run short.

Friends,

Because of this war, fertiliser prices around the world have risen sharply. The chemicals used in producing fertilisers have also become much more expensive. Yet the government did not allow this burden to fall on farmers. A bag of urea that costs around ₹3,000 elsewhere in the world is available to Indian farmers for less than ₹300. The global price of a bag of urea is around ₹3,000, but the government bears that burden and provides it to you for around ₹300. The price of a bag of DAP fertiliser has crossed ₹5,000 globally. But Indian farmers receive the same bag for around ₹1,350. The nation is providing this support so that our farmers become stronger and their lives improve.

Friends,

In a world full of uncertainty, India’s rapid development has become a new source of hope for the entire world. In such a situation, we must continue moving forward on the path of Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat – One India, Great India. And tomorrow, the 31st of October, is a day to strengthen this resolve. Tomorrow is the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and National Unity Day. The entire nation will celebrate National Unity Day. On this day, the Run for Unity is organised across the country. Reports are coming in from all directions about the grand preparations being made for the Run for Unity. I would especially urge all citizens of the country, particularly our young friends, to participate enthusiastically in the Run for Unity tomorrow morning.

Friends,

Every year, the Unity Festival is celebrated in Ekta Nagar on the morning of 31st October. But this year, keeping the Run for Unity and other programmes in mind, it will be held in the evening instead of the morning. This is a change from previous years. Tomorrow at 5:30 in the evening, a grand Unity Festival will be celebrated in Ekta Nagar. The programme will be organised on a very large scale. You should watch it on television. There will be such a parade on the soil of Gujarat that it will remind you of the Republic Day celebrations in Delhi. Do watch it. There will be parades by police and security forces, and impressive tableaux will be displayed. I urge all citizens of the country to join this programme tomorrow evening as well. From Kashmir to Kanyakumari, from Kutch to Kamakhya, the entire nation should pay tribute to Sardar Patel and reaffirm the resolve of Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat. With this appeal, I once again extend my best wishes to all of you for these development works.

Thank you very much.

The sisters seated at the back are offering their blessings to me. Mothers, I bow at your feet. Your blessings give me tremendous strength. I am deeply grateful to all of you.

Bharat Mata Ki Jai!

Bharat Mata Ki Jai!
texts.pms-address-during-inauguration-of-the-e:
Union Minister in my Cabinet Dr. Jitendra Singh ji, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India Ajay Sood ji, all Nobel Prize-winning scientists, all other distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen.

Today, such a large number of delegates from the world of Science and Technology are present here. Our young innovators are here as well. Before coming here, I interacted with some startup founders. The scale at which India’s youth are thinking and the confidence with which they are moving forward is truly encouraging.

Friends,

I had attended this conclave last time as well. This time, we are discussing the subject of Emerging Science and Technology. Decades ago, there was a time when Science and Technology, for India, meant catching up. Whenever something new was innovated in the world, that technology would reach us after a few years. We would adopt it or make minor improvements and move forward. But today, 21st-century India is moving ahead with a new mindset and a new confidence. Now our goal is to create new technologies for India, for the world, for today, and for the future, to determine their direction, and to develop the capability to provide solutions to global challenges. During the COVID period, we saw an example of this. When many countries around the world were struggling with vaccine availability, India developed its own vaccine, carried out vaccination on a large scale, and also supplied vaccines to other nations. This is the confidence of 21st-century India. We reach Mars in our very first attempt. We reach the South Pole of the Moon, a place where no one had reached before. And that is why I firmly believe: India must embrace the technologies of the future, innovate boldly, and lead the world in creating them.

Friends,

From the discovery of zero to the number system and astronomy, India’s tradition has always been one of knowledge and discovery. Today, we are taking this scientific heritage forward with modern technologies and renewed confidence. Some examples from the past year help us understand this transformation even better. On 30th October, the nation will celebrate the birth anniversary of Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha. Therefore, let me begin with nuclear energy.

Friends,

All of you know that for building a Developed India, we will require nuclear energy on a large scale. Dependence on imports for nuclear fuel is a challenge to our energy security. Therefore, India is rapidly advancing its Fast Breeder Reactor Technology. Just a few months ago, the country’s 500-Megawatt Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor achieved First Criticality. This is an extremely significant and important step towards strengthening our long-term capabilities in the field of nuclear energy.

Friends,

Whether it is energy security or self-reliance in technology, India’s goal is not limited to fulfilling its own needs. Our objective is also to expand our strength in critical technologies. This year, India achieved new milestones in the space sector as well. An Indian space startup successfully placed a satellite into orbit using a Made-in-India rocket in its very first attempt. India also achieved the capability of satellite docking. Today, many Indian startups are bringing new solutions in space science. The participation of young scientists and entrepreneurs in the space sector is also increasing significantly.

Friends,

The range of achievements India is making across various sectors is unprecedented. This very year, India hosted the AI Impact Summit and launched its own AI model. The first shipments of chips manufactured in India have now started reaching global markets. In the field of battery storage as well, we are working on capacity building based on raw materials available within India itself.

Friends,

From nuclear energy to space, and from AI to semiconductors, the requirements of these sectors are different. But their message is one and the same. India is strengthening both its capabilities and its confidence in emerging technologies. India possesses another strength as well: solutions at scale. Whenever a solution succeeds in India, it creates pathways for solving the problems of many countries around the world. Our Digital Stack is a wonderful example of this. Our 5G technology is another example. India is moving towards developing secure solutions that can reach people on a large scale.

Friends,

You all know that one challenge in the world of Science and Technology has always been the tendency to see it as a weapon. India, however, believes that Science and Technology are instruments for the service of humanity. The true success of science comes when it moves from the laboratory into the lives of ordinary citizens and improves them. Lab to land, the success of this technology is not determined merely by how advanced it is. Its real strength lies in how large a problem it solves and how many lives it transforms. Therefore, for us, Emerging Science and Technology means solutions that strengthen healthcare, transform agriculture, create new opportunities in education and employment, and help in disaster management. I am pleased that India’s startup revolution is giving prominence to such questions. One startup is working on wearable EEG technology that helps understand brain activity. Indian companies are developing indigenous wireless and satellite communication solutions. In the field of nutrition, products are being developed keeping special dietary needs in mind. Indian companies are working on new technologies in the semiconductor sector. Solutions for utilising industrial waste such as steel slag are also being explored in our country.

Friends,

Just a few days ago, I had the opportunity to visit Chennai. I would like to share that experience with you as well. There, I inaugurated a modern Brain Centre at IIT Madras. This centre has developed a brain imaging technology platform that is a model for the entire world. This Brain Centre is working on developing high-resolution digital 3D images of the human brain. The success of this mission will help solve many complexities associated with neurological diseases. Science for Society, Technology for Transformation, this should be the benchmark of our scientific progress. And India is moving forward while measuring itself against this benchmark.

Friends,

We all know that a country’s technology and technology-creation capability depends on its research. Research is the power that enables a nation to find solutions to its own problems and become self-reliant in critical technologies. That is why I have said: Jai Vigyan, Jai Anusandhan! For a Developed India, we are continuously strengthening our research sector. With this resolve, the Anusandhan National Research Foundation is being accelerated. Last year, on this very platform, we pledged an allocation of one lakh crore rupees for Research, Development, and Innovation. Today, the results are becoming visible. In the past year, nearly twelve thousand crore rupees have already been committed to technologies that are ready to move from the laboratory to the market. And private investors are participating equally in this effort. Alongside the government’s commitment of twelve thousand crore rupees, the private sector is also investing twelve thousand crore rupees. This means that within just one year, a total new commitment of twenty-four thousand crore rupees has been made towards Research and Development.

Friends,

India’s research ecosystem is also continuously expanding. Patent applications have seen substantial growth. Ten years ago, fewer than fifty thousand patent applications were filed in an entire year. Last year, this number rose to nearly one hundred and fifty thousand. These figures do not merely indicate rising numbers. They signify a transformation in which research and innovation are emerging as a strong culture within India.

Friends,

In this second quarter of the 21st century, another question has become extremely important. In the age of AI, how will scientific judgement evolve? The scientists leading our laboratories have developed their expertise through years of experience. On this stage too, several distinguished scientists and Nobel laureates are present. We all know that they developed their understanding by solving small problems, conducting experiments, and learning from failures. A scientist does not merely repeat available information. A scientist questions established patterns. A scientist examines solutions from new perspectives. A scientist identifies aspects that others may have overlooked. It is through this process that scientific judgement develops. Today, however, in the age of AI, a new challenge is emerging before us. AI can complete many routine tasks very quickly. This can improve research productivity. But we must also ensure that AI does not limit scientific thinking and independent judgement, but instead enriches them. The time saved through AI should be used for addressing more challenging problems, conducting new experiments, and testing new ideas. AI can provide answers quickly. But the responsibility of verifying the truth of those answers must remain with the scientist.

Friends,

We must continue preparing our scientists and institutions not only for today’s needs but also for future challenges. Semiconductors, Quantum Technologies, Biotechnology, Advanced Materials, Robotics, Space, Clean Energy, and Next-Generation Communications are areas that will shape the future. India is building strong scientific foundations in all these fields. For this purpose, several National Missions have also been launched. Our objective is that new breakthroughs in these domains should emerge from India as well. And our responsibility extends beyond innovation alone. Whether it is AI, synthetic biology, or autonomous systems, safety and security must be given priority. In the age of AI, new challenges and new threats are also emerging in cybersecurity. From our financial networks to our national security systems, everyone faces this challenge. Therefore, it is essential that we work on AI-based solutions and advance quantum security solutions that can secure the country’s systems against these threats. Our goal is to develop technologies that strengthen India while also contributing solutions to the challenges facing humanity.

Friends,

I appeal to every researcher, industry leader, startup founder, and young student present at this conclave to set a concrete goal for themselves. In the next three years, what technology, prototype, pilot project, or product will they contribute towards developing? Let us create innovations that support the making of a Developed India. Let us create innovations that make India a centre point for global solutions. Therefore, it is my hope that this conclave does not remain limited to an exchange of ideas alone. It should become a platform for measurable outcomes.

Friends,

Today, India is the youngest country in the world. We have talent. We have the resolve to create something new. We must build a generation that does not merely participate in Emerging Science and Technology, but leads it. Our spirit should be: We will do it. We will do it. Our confidence should be: We will do it. Once again, I extend my very best wishes for the success of this conclave.

Thank you!
texts.pms-address-during-inauguration-key-rbi-:
Jai Jagannath.

Governor of Odisha, Shri Brajmohan Ram ji; popular Chief Minister of the state, Shri Mohan Charan Majhi ji; my colleagues in the Union Government, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman ji, Shri Jual Oram ji; Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, Shri Sanjay Malhotra ji; Deputy Chief Ministers of Odisha, Smt. Pravati Parida ji, Shri Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo ji; distinguished guests associated with the banking and financial sector, ladies and gentlemen.

Why is the atmosphere so serious? Does banking carry this much pressure, does technology carry this much pressure? Please sit comfortably.

With the blessings of Mahaprabhu, today Bhubaneswar is giving a new institution to a New India. The inauguration of both the RBI’s Data Centre and the Cybersecurity Training Institute in Bhubaneswar marks an important occasion. This is going to be of immense benefit to the people of Odisha and the entire country. I extend my heartiest congratulations to the RBI and everyone associated with this project.

Friends,

Today’s programme bears testimony to how the approach to governance in India is transforming and how rapidly it is evolving. And our focus within this is: priority of development, expansion of development, and reaching the last person with development.

Friends,

After independence, large cities were developed in the country, grand institutions were established, large hospitals were built, and massive airports were constructed. Yet, a vast section of the country kept waiting for basic amenities. Delhi had large hospitals, but people in smaller cities and remote areas had to travel long distances for better medical treatment. Large cities enjoyed air travel facilities, but connecting smaller towns with air connectivity was not given adequate focus. Big cities had some amenities, whereas in numerous villages, meeting basic needs such as roads, electricity, and water remained a formidable challenge. Railway stations formed the most crucial link of the common citizen’s travel, yet modern amenities were lacking at these stations. In other words, ensuring that the benefits of development reached every region and every citizen equally remained a major hurdle. We made an effort to transform this very mindset. We proceeded with a model of Pro-People, Pro-Active, Good Governance. For us, development denotes balanced progress across India – opportunities for villages as well as smaller towns. Our goal is to extend better connectivity to far-flung areas, provide facilities for underprivileged families to live with dignity, and continually instill confidence in every citizen that they will not be left behind in the journey of development. Today, the nation’s expressways are linking smaller cities. Premier institutions like AIIMS have expanded across multiple states. Medical colleges are being opened in smaller towns. Nearly 1.75 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs have been established in villages. Digital connectivity is expanding into remote regions. This is the true purpose of governance now: making citizens’ lives easier and offering new avenues for their aspirations.

Friends,

Our banking sector has also stood as a prime example of how ordinary families, the poor, and the middle class were kept deprived for decades. In the 1960s and 70s, banks were nationalised in the name of the poor. Yet, until 2014, more than half of the country’s population was excluded from the banking ecosystem. Financial products such as bank loans were a distant dream even for the middle class; the poor, small farmers, the landless, and our sisters and daughters could not even fathom accessing them. Today, digital banking in India has connected everyone to 24-hour financial services. But prior to 2014, there was an entirely different era of ‘phone banking’. A select few in Delhi and those connected with influential circles were granted loans worth thousands of crores through phone calls. Poor and middle-class families required a guarantor merely to open a single bank account, whereas under the Congress’s phone banking arrangement, thousands of crores of rupees were available anytime for the wealthy. It was the consequence of this very mismanagement that pushed India’s banking system into the grip of NPAs, driving it to the brink of ruin.

Friends,

For any substantial transformation, having an expansive mindset is essential; when intentions are pure and motives are noble, tasks that seem impossible turn into reality. Where vision is narrow, possibilities also shrink. The frameworks built by the nation in recent years, along with the new ecosystem developed under Digital India, have extended banking to every single citizen. Today, India’s banking sector stands among the strongest in the world. Earlier, through phone banking, only those with access to a privileged family in Delhi benefited. Today, through digital banking, every household across the nation has become a beneficiary.

Friends,

It was from this very land of Odisha that a former Prime Minister of the country once stated that when one rupee is sent from Delhi, only 15 paise reaches the people. That was a statement from a Prime Minister. That was one era, and this is today. Today, when one rupee leaves Delhi, the entire one rupee reaches the bank account of every beneficiary. As Nirmala ji mentioned just now, this has been made possible solely because of the approximately 59 to 60 crore Jan Dhan accounts opened in the country.

Friends,

Today, even someone who has nothing to offer the bank as a guarantee is able to secure an affordable and accessible loan to start their own work. From small entrepreneurs to traditional artisans, from street vendors to workers in the unorganised sector, they have received the benefits of formal banking for the first time. Through the Mudra Yojana, 13 crore people have become first-time entrepreneurs. PM SVANidhi has provided loans to lakhs of street vendors for the first time. The PM Vishwakarma scheme has connected lakhs of skilled craftspersons with banks. Banks have also extended assistance worth thousands of crores of rupees to self-help groups comprising 10 crore rural women.

Friends,

This is the same nation where debit and credit cards were once symbols reserved for the wealthy. Today, they are accessible to every citizen. Crores of RuPay credit and debit cards have been issued in the country, becoming symbols of both self-respect and self-reliance. All of this has been achieved through your collective cooperation. Be it the RBI, every bank in the nation, or each bank employee serving within them – the work you have accomplished makes you truly deserving of this success.

Friends,

Over the past decade, alongside financial empowerment, the social security net has witnessed an unprecedented expansion. Through the Atal Pension Yojana, 9 crore people have received social security coverage, with 38 lakh individuals covered in Odisha alone. About 10 to 12 years ago, insurance was considered a luxury; the poor and middle class could hardly contemplate it. For us, ‘Nagrik Devo Bhava’ (The Citizen is Divine) is the guiding mantra of good governance. To provide protection during accidents, we introduced the PM Suraksha Bima Yojana. At a nominal premium of just ₹20 per year, an insurance coverage of up to ₹2 lakh is being provided. Similarly, for life insurance, we introduced the PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, available at an annual premium of less than ₹450. Crores of Indians are enrolled in both these schemes. To date, claims exceeding ₹25,000 crore have been disbursed to the public. If any other government had announced the distribution of ₹25,000 crore, it would have generated massive headlines, accompanied by celebrations and fanfares for months. However, under our administration, this support reaches the poor and the middle class during difficult times silently and without fanfare. This is what defines good governance.

Friends,

The past decade focused on extending banking access to those who were excluded. The coming decade belongs to making banking more efficient and more dependable. In this effort, this new Data Centre in Odisha will play a major role. If we are to keep the banking system secure, its digital infrastructure must also remain protected. For this reason, we require robust data centres and empowered computing systems.

And friends,

We all understand that modern warfare is not waged solely with weapons. Weakening a country can also be attempted by striking at its economy. As India gains financial strength, safeguarding our banking system against cyber criminals and cyber terrorists is equally imperative. The nature of cyber threats is evolving today. We cannot counter such emerging challenges using outdated systems, obsolete training modules, or legacy tools. This necessitates modern infrastructure alongside skilled human resources. It is precisely here that the role of this new Cybersecurity Training Institute becomes critically important.

Friends,

These new facilities of the RBI also reflect a fresh priority for India. Eastern India is emerging as a powerful growth engine for a developed India. Following the formation of the double-engine government in Odisha, progress has gained new momentum. Alongside its natural resources, Odisha’s economy is now being fortified by technology. On one hand, mineral-based industries are expanding; on the other hand, concerted efforts are underway to foster a new ecosystem for semiconductors and electronics. You will witness that Odisha is set to script a new future, spanning from mines to microchips. Fresh investment prospects are emerging in Odisha across data centres and advanced computing, opening numerous avenues for its youth. I assure the young people of Odisha that the big dreams you have envisioned will certainly be fulfilled. We will do it; we are determined to accomplish this. With this spirit, I once again extend my heartfelt congratulations to all of you.

Best wishes to everyone.

Jai Jagannath!
texts.pms-address-at-the-inauguration-of-chinm:
Most revered Pujya Swami Tejomayananda ji, Pujya Swami Swaroopananda ji, Pujya Swami Mitrananda ji, Pujya Swami Viviktananda ji, all revered saints, Acharyas, all dedicated sevaks of Chinmaya Mission, devotees and seekers who have arrived from across the country and abroad, ladies and gentlemen.

Courtesy of all of you, today I have had the opportunity to participate in the Amrit Mahotsav of Chinmaya Mission. This is a unique spiritual experience. This is the special affection and blessing of our saints towards me. Because the Chinmaya Mission is not merely an institution; it is a Chinmaya ideal, which was established by a Chinmaya Rishi. Its journey over several decades has also been replete with pure, conscious resolutions. And whatever is Chinmaya is naturally immortal and imbued with nectar. Therefore, today at Bharat Mandapam, the name of this event – ‘Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav’ – is equally meaningful. I extend my heartiest congratulations on the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav to the saints and Acharyas associated with the Chinmaya Mission across the globe, and to lakhs of seekers and followers.

Friends,

The feeling that arose in my heart upon arriving here today was made even more vibrant through modern technology. The darshan of Pujya Gurudev Swami Chinmayananda ji in this form, the privilege of conversing with his holobot, made it feel as though I had travelled 33 years back in time. My meeting with Gurudev in Vadodara in 1993, the conversation with him, his affection, his blessings – today everything reappeared before my eyes once again. For a moment, it felt as though I was once again in the direct physical presence of Gurudev. For me, this is a deeply emotional experience. I thank all the members of Chinmaya Mission from the bottom of my heart for this wonderful experience, and express my gratitude to them.

Friends,

Around February-March in 1993, I met Pujya Gurudev; I had gone to invite him to the centenary celebrations of the Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago, USA. At that very time, 100 years of Swami Vivekananda ji’s historic address were being marked. Pujya Gurudev accepted the invitation; Pujya Gurudev went to America, and across various programmes there, he consistently made people aware of the centenary celebrations of the World’s Parliament of Religions and inspired them to take part. But destiny had ordained otherwise. Just a few weeks prior to the Parliament of Religions, on 3 August, Gurudev shed his mortal body in San Diego, America, leaving all of us behind. When the Parliament of Religions took place in Chicago on 11 September, fortunately, I was there. All of us felt the absence of Pujya Gurudev. Many words spoken by Gurudev kept echoing in my mind. The profound discussion that took place during my last meeting with him remains etched in my memory even today. Its core sentiment was: the building of youth power! And, through youth power, the creation of an empowered and capable India.

Friends,

A few years after meeting him, the sovereign people blessed me with the opportunity to serve as the Chief Minister of Gujarat. Since then until today, for the past 25 years, as the head of the government, I have been continuously serving the nation to the best of my ability; Guruji’s blessings are with me. In this journey, the youth of the country stand at the centre of my efforts and policies. I am delighted that at the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav as well, the youth have shouldered major responsibilities. Many of our young companions undertook a journey of 40,000 kilometres over nearly 300 days. During this period, more than one lakh youths were contacted. I congratulate the entire team for this remarkable endeavour as well.

Friends,

The declaration of our Upanishads is: “Vayam Amritasya Putrah”. That is, we are the children of immortality. This conception is not merely a spiritual philosophy; it is also our cultural conviction. This does not mean that our physical bodies are immortal; it means our consciousness is immortal. Our knowledge and our awareness are immortal. Because of this very awareness, this India has remained immortal for thousands of years. Because the very meaning of the word ‘Bharat’ is that which is engaged in the pursuit of knowledge and illumination.

Therefore, friends,

When the occasion of 75 years of the country’s independence arrived, the thought came to my mind that we must not only turn this occasion into an inspirational platform for a developed India, but we must also revive that essence of India which knows how to live with immortal ideas, and which, through its experience of thousands of centuries, can care for humanity across eras. That is why I called for celebrating that occasion as the Amrit Mahotsav. And see, with the passage of time, one wondrous journey after another has continued to align with that resolution. Numerous spiritual, cultural, and social organisations took Amrit resolves at key milestones of their respective journeys during this period. And now, Chinmaya Mission is also joining the mission of India’s Amrit Kaal in the form of its Amrit Mahotsav. And this indeed is the true strength of India’s resolves; this is the genuine proof of our being “Amritasya Putrah”.

Friends,

The call of our Vedas is: “Vayam Rashtre Jagriyama Purohitah” – meaning, may we, who seek the welfare of the nation, keep the nation awakened and elevated. Swami Chinmayananda ji lived his entire life guided by this very mantra. With as much devotion as he spoke on spiritual matters, with equal promptness he delivered articulate discourses on national issues. Because our nation is the birthplace of our culture. This nation is the very foundation of our existence. Swamiji always taught that we should link our spiritual advancement with personal growth, and make personal growth the vehicle for national progress. To fill the people of India with self-respect towards India was Swamiji’s mission. With this objective, he initiated the Gita Jnana Yajna. He began the campaign of taking the wisdom of the Upanishads, Vedanta, and our scriptures to the common people. And today, we can see the results of that resolution of his in many ways. Due to the efforts of Chinmaya Mission, today there are lakhs of youth who are serving as cultural brand ambassadors of India. These youth are passing on Indian values to the new generation. This contribution of Pujya Gurudev is an important chapter in India’s cultural and spiritual renaissance.

Friends,

Today, I also recall the occasion of Pujya Gurudev’s birth centenary. In 2015, I had the privilege of releasing a special commemorative coin in his memory. Even then, I had remarked that Swamiji’s life was a wonderful confluence of knowledge, action, and devotion. His Guru, Swami Sivananda ji, had blessed him with the words: “Go, roar like a lion.” He lived his entire life in that very spirit. The confidence and inner strength in his speech left an enduring impression of his thoughts on everyone’s heart. His radio programme named ‘Art of Man Making’ provided direction to countless individuals.

Friends,

The mission of great personalities remains alive even after they depart. That is why today we see that more than 100 educational institutions of Chinmaya Mission are shaping the future of lakhs of children and youth. In these institutions, they are receiving modern education while also assimilating Indian values.

Friends,

The vision that visionary individuals like Swami Chinmayananda ji held at the time of independence – today the nation is fulfilling its responsibilities in that very direction. To ensure that our education system aligns with the needs of a new India, we introduced the National Education Policy. In this new Education Policy, priority has been accorded to Indian knowledge traditions, education in the mother tongue, modern science, and new technology.

Friends,

Another mission of Swamiji’s life was: pride in Indian heritage and its preservation! All of you are familiar with the Vivekananda Rock Memorial in Kanyakumari. The resolution to build a memorial on that massive rock amidst the sea was taken by Shri Eknath Ranade ji. At that time, Pujya Gurudev stood firmly by his side. The first financial contribution for this great endeavour was also made by Pujya Swamiji. Today, the Vivekananda Rock Memorial stands as a centre of inspiration for lakhs of people visiting from across the country and the world.

Friends,

Today, from north to south, east to west, India’s cultural centres are undergoing a renaissance. Be it the renewed form of Kashi Vishwanath Dham, the grand temple of Lord Shri Ram in Ayodhya, the Mahakal Mahalok of Ujjain, or our shrines like Kedarnath and Badrinath. If you have visited Kedarnath ji recently, a divine, grand statue of Adi Shankar, Adi Shankaracharya ji, has been established there, where Adi Shankar shed his mortal coil. Today, they are returning to their majestic form. All of you know that at one time, so many statues were stolen from India, taken abroad, and sold there. There was no one to stop it, no one to inquire – leave aside those who worshipped them, there was no one even to ask. Over the past 12 years, we have brought back more than six hundred and fifty such stolen ancient statues. Our cultural centres are becoming part of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Friends,

Just as Swamiji took our dharma and philosophy to the people of the world, similarly, today International Yoga Day is connecting people across the globe with India and with our ancient, glorious tradition. This confidence of taking pride in our heritage, this assurance of liberation from the mindset of subjugation, is evidence that the nation is now advancing on the path envisioned for centuries by our rishis and patriots. Their strength of thought is our greatest asset along this path.

Friends,

Different institutions and organisations have their respective objectives, but the one purpose that unites everyone, the destination where all paths converge, that goal is: the development of the nation, the pride of the nation. In Swami Chinmayananda ji’s time, according to the challenges that lay before the country, he shaped his resolutions. In the passing decades, times have changed, new challenges have arisen before the nation, and new distortions have entered society. Today, the responsibility of finding solutions rests upon all of us. Today, we have to unite society against divisive forces, and make our fellow citizens aware of self-reliance. We have to connect every individual with the resolution of a Developed India by 2047. We must become even more proactive towards these objectives.

Friends,

In 2047, when India completes 100 years of its independence, around that very period, Chinmaya Mission will also celebrate its centenary year. That is to say, Chinmaya Mission’s centenary journey and the journey towards a Developed India will progress together. Therefore, our goals are one, our objectives are one, and we must take this journey forward together. You possess the great legacy of Gurudev and decades of experience. You have a vast family of dedicated Acharyas, seekers, and workers across the globe. I am confident that all of you together will play an important role in building a Developed India. With this conviction, I once again bow at the feet of Pujya Gurudev. I extend my heartiest congratulations on the Amrit Mahotsav to all the saints, Acharyas, seekers, and service-oriented companions of Chinmaya Mission.

Hari Om.

Hari Om.

Hari Om.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-address-during-participation-in-ndtv:
Greetings to all of you! This is the festive season; the nation is filled with celebration, enthusiasm, and energy. In this atmosphere of joy and celebration, I welcome and greet all of you friends who have come here from all over the world.

Friends,

This NDTV summit is dedicated to deliberating on serious matters. Nowadays, everyone is talking about a new world order. Because this affects ordinary life, the importance of such world summits increases even more.

Friends

When talking about ‘The World Between Orders’, we need to understand two things. First, why is the world order changing? Why is the old global order unable to provide solutions to today’s challenges? And second, what is India’s role in this changing world?

Friends,

If I elaborate on the first point, this change is natural and spontaneous. The Second World War taught the world a major lesson. The world realized that a global order cannot function merely on the basis of power and self-interest. Dialogue is essential, cooperation is necessary, and resolving disputes is equally vital. It was this sentiment that laid the foundation of the United Nations, or the UN. For decades, the UN played a significant role in promoting global cooperation and peace. But with time, the world kept changing. New aspirations emerged. New economies and new powers arose. The challenges confronting the world also became far more complex than ever before. Technology transformed society, the economy, and the very nature of power. And countries that were not at the table when the global order was initially established came forward with their own prominent roles. The question then arises: did the global order change at the same pace? The answer is no. Neither did the world order change, nor could global institutions adapt themselves with equivalent speed. The United Nations and other global institutions have had their historic role. Yet in the face of today’s challenges, their limitations are clearly visible. Now, emerging powers are rising. New voices are demanding their rightful place. New challenges demand new solutions. When the reality of the world shifts, but decision-making methods remain unchanged, a gap begins to widen between the system and reality. That is precisely what we are witnessing today. For decades, trade connected nations, technology closed distances, maritime routes linked economies, and culture and mobility brought diverse societies closer together; but today, these very links face fresh strains. Trade is being weaponized. Technology is turning into a new arena of competition and conflict. Sea routes are emerging as epicenters of geopolitical tension. Therefore, the challenge today is not merely about the emergence of a new global order. The real challenge is: in a changing world, how do we build an order where new realities find their place, global institutions become more effective, and the spirit of cooperation among nations is reinforced? And this is where the question of India’s role comes to the fore.

Friends,

Before elaborating on India’s role, I will take you back by 7 to 8 years. What transpired during the COVID pandemic is something we all witnessed. When the world needed cooperation the most, it appeared completely divided. Those who made grand proclamations about globalization prioritized their own self-interests in a time of crisis. In that era of fragmentation, everyone viewed each other with suspicion, and global trust had hit rock bottom; it was then, in 2020, from the G20 platform, that I placed an idea before the world, calling for “a new world order for the collective well-being of humankind” – an order with humanity at its very core. That same year, from the UNGA platform, I said, “If the century changes and we do not, our ability to bring about change also weakens.”

Friends,

Today, while it is true that the world order is changing, the real question is: as the old global order shifts, what kind of new world order do we want to build together? Reforms in multilateral institutions are essential. It is vital to grant the Global South its rightful place and voice. International cooperation must not be reserved only for good times; it must remain effective during crises, and for this, meaningful consensus among all stakeholders is imperative.

Friends,

In our heritage, Chanakya stated in the Arthashastra: ‘Apranitah tu matsya-nyayam ud-bhavayati’ – meaning, when governance weakens, the “law of the fish” (matsya nyaya) takes over. Under matsya nyaya, the big fish swallows the smaller fish. The world needs a system that prevents such a situation from arising. That is India’s vision, and that is precisely what India is doing. The world experienced this role of India during the severe crisis of the pandemic. When capable nations were thinking solely of themselves, India stepped forward, delivered vaccines to every needy nation, and dispatched medicines to over 100 countries.

Friends,

Guided by the principle of ‘Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas’, India is performing its duty as a Vishwa-Bandhu (universal friend). You have witnessed this firsthand: the G20 Summit was held under India’s presidency, and the BRICS Summit was held under India’s leadership. How many doubts were voiced regarding both summits? It was said that building consensus on joint declarations would be impossible. But India built bridges, emphasized dialogue, and on both occasions, the Delhi Declaration was adopted through unanimous consensus. Nations considered bitter rivals came together on India’s platform. This is not mere coincidence. This is the trust placed in India’s role as a Vishwa-Bandhu.

Friends,

The stronger and more empowered India becomes, the greater the benefit to humanity. This is because India’s policies and decisions are inspired by timeless experience and civilizational values. India does not make decisions driven by fleeting moments. Hence, India is a guarantee of stability and an assurance of continuity. Our resolve for a Viksit Bharat (Developed India) also fosters this very spirit. Just a few days ago at a summit, I presented the vision of “Power to Empower.” A developed India is not just for ourselves; it is a guarantee for a better world. When India advances toward self-reliance, it strengthens global supply chains. When India’s economy grows stronger, it provides hope of prosperity to the world. When India’s youth become capable and skilled, it inspires global confidence in innovation and productivity. In other words, India is enhancing its own capabilities today so that the world’s capacity can also increase.

Friends,

India is working with all its might to become a top-3 economy. Our confidence grows even further when we look at the present difficult global circumstances, in the midst of which India continues to emerge as the fastest-growing major economy. Today, India is among the top economies in green energy. India ranks among the top three AI ecosystems. India is among the top three startup ecosystems. India is one of the largest digital economies. India stands number one in real-time digital payments.

Friends,

Today’s India is expanding its capabilities across various sectors, and there are numerous milestones achieved for the first time in the country. India’s Fast Breeder Reactor achieved criticality for the first time. India linked the Census with digital technology for the first time. During this period, India’s first hydrogen train began operations, and India crossed the 300-gigawatt mark in non-fossil electricity capacity for the first time.

Friends,

I will give you another example. A few days ago, I had the opportunity to meet young athletes returning from the Asian Games. India won 85 medals this time, achieving many milestones for the first time. The women’s recurve archery team won team and individual gold medals for the first time. In boxing, India won three gold medals in a single Asian Games, which is also a first.

Friends,

Now I will mention a term, and I hope many people in the hall have heard it. The word is – Sepak Takraw. Sepak Takraw, have you heard this word? For those who do not know, let me tell you that it is the name of a sport. The world plays it and has been winning medals in it. It is essentially a hybrid combination of football and volleyball. It is played with the feet, but the action takes place across a net. India won a medal for the first time in recent Asian Games in an event of this sport – the Men’s Quadrant.

Friends,

This is the hallmark of a changing India. In every sector, something new and unprecedented is taking place. That means India’s conventional strengths are being reinforced, and where we were once not as strong, we are emerging as a new force. None of this is happening in isolation; it is the direct outcome of the policy of ‘Reform, Perform, Transform’.

Friends,

The country has seen days when the entire power grid would collapse under rising electricity demand. But when a nation rises with sheer willpower and sets forth, the power grid does not collapse; instead, that very grid fuels the nation’s progress and soaring confidence.

Friends,

Today, our youth power, women power, our farmers, fishermen, the poor, and the middle class are engaged with high spirits in the building of a Viksit Bharat. Look around today: India’s exports are setting new records. Speaking of September alone, exports of goods and products increased by nearly 25 percent compared to last year. Seafood exports have more than doubled in the last 12 years. In our villages, more than 3.5 crore women have become Lakhpati Didis, and we are working toward the goal of creating 6 crore Lakhpati Didis. Under the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana, around 70 lakh new jobs have been created in a very short span of time. For the middle class, income tax has been made zero up to 12 lakh rupees – this needs to be reminded to you again and again; it cannot be that you simply take what you get and forget it. Ease of Living is improving across the country, and new employment opportunities are being generated.

Friends,

There was a time when the world referred to India as the ‘World’s Back Office’, but today’s India is not merely a service provider; we are innovating, designing, and creating new solutions and technologies for the world. Look at the field of research alone: today we rank third in research publications. In the year 2025, nearly 1.5 lakh patents were filed – 1.5 lakh patents in a single year. This offers a glimpse into the immense potential for research and innovation in India.

Friends,

Consider the semiconductor sector as well: nearly 20 percent of the world’s chip-design workforce is in India. Indian engineers within the country are working on advanced 2 to 3-nanometer chip designs. To expand this talent pool further, every necessary facility is being provided in the country today. In Indian academic institutions, our students have designed more than 325 chips so far.

Friends,

Another example is Global Capability Centres. More than half of the world’s capability centres are located in India. It is not just about the numbers; the nature of their work is changing. Previously, many centres focused solely on support services. Today, they operate across fields like AI, Cloud, Engineering, Analytics, and Product Development. In other words, India’s role is shifting, and India’s identity is evolving. We have moved from ‘Talent at Scale’ to ‘Thinking at Scale’. The world that once trusted India’s manpower now places equal trust in India’s mind-power. As a result, we are working alongside the world not merely as a Back Office, but as a Brain Office.

Friends,

Whenever the government frames a policy or takes an investment decision in any sector, there is clear thinking behind it: what capacities India needs to develop, in which domains we must reduce dependence on other nations, and which impending crises we must prepare for today. We keep these factors in mind with every decision. There are many investments whose benefits take years to become visible, but they hold immense significance for the nation’s future. Let me share an interesting example. All of you are familiar with India’s pharmaceutical capabilities, but until a few years ago, India relied heavily on imports for raw materials and medicines. Now the country is changing this situation. You must have heard of Penicillin G, which is essential for antibiotics. Over the last two to three decades, its domestic production in India had practically ceased. We brought it under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme. Today, after many years, domestic production of Penicillin G has resumed in Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh.

Friends,

Penicillin G is just one example. In India, we are building an entire domestic supply chain for APIs (Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients) – the fundamental raw materials for medicine manufacturing. That is why this sector was brought under the PLI scheme, attracting over 5,000 crore rupees in investment so far, with around 40 projects already underway. Such policies and decisions are steering India toward self-reliance.

Friends,

Amidst discussions of so many national achievements, our media friends might complain that while much was said, nothing was spoken about their work. NDTV is hosting such a magnificent event, and our motto is ‘Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas’ – which includes the development of the media – so perhaps you would appreciate a few candid and sweet-and-sour remarks as well?

Friends,

While the world is searching for a new order, some people are dreaming of disorder in India. Today, when there is so much disarray in the world, the image of a strong India should be conveyed globally. Yet these individuals are bent on tarnishing India’s reputation. They travel abroad to defame India and plead for foreign intervention. One wonders how long Congress will continue to wager the nation’s interests just to launch its failed product. In an entire year, Sriharikota does not attempt as many launches as Congress makes failed attempts to launch its leader.

Friends,

Whatever decline Congress chooses to bring upon itself is entirely its own concern, and we have no problem with that. But to protect one family from the repeated stain of failure, Congress is putting India’s achievements, strengths, and progress on trial. The grapes are so sour that Congress has set about cutting down the grapevine itself. In reality, this family has become a burden on their party; senior elders of the party understand this and even share it with us in private, yet they swallow their humiliation and remain silent.

Friends,

This conduct of Congress harms honest critics of the government as well, and this imposes a huge cost in a democracy. Honest critics suffer immensely because of this. Those who wish to present their critique against the government in a democratic manner find their voices drowned out by Congress’s clamour; the voices of genuine critics are suppressed. Those who genuinely care for democracy and the national interest—even if they are staunch opponents of the government—find no opportunity to speak amidst the shouting and screeching of Congress. We have seen in Parliament: there are so many talented young Members of Parliament from opposition parties who wish to put forward their views and critique the government, but Congress disrupts Parliament so that others do not get an opportunity, simply because Congress wants to keep only one person in the limelight. By doing so, Congress does a grave injustice to the young MPs of the opposition.

And friends,

Movements that organically aim to highlight the government’s shortcomings and genuinely seek systemic reform—which is indeed necessary in a democracy—are also ruined by Congress. Congress has become a parasite that does not want anyone else to progress. Intellectual Naxals have captured Congress’s mind to such an extent that Congress has lost its own capacity to think. Those who once wrought destruction in forests have infiltrated Congress and are now bent on wreaking havoc on the country.

Friends,

Amidst all these challenges, the grand goal of a Viksit Bharat stands before us. The nation’s aspirations are boundless. Therefore, a single spirit resonates across India today, and that spirit is: ‘We Will Do It, We Will Do It.’ We will dream big, turn every challenge into an opportunity, and translate every resolution into reality. Our strength is our self-confidence; our inspiration lies in the dreams of 140 crore fellow citizens. We will innovate, forge new paths, reach new heights, and link India’s success with the world’s success. I am confident that the nectar emerging from this summit will empower this very spirit, infuse our resolutions with new energy, and play a vital role in realizing India’s grand aspirations. Once again, my warmest wishes to all of you.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-press-statement-during-joint-press-s:
Your Excellency, Mr. Prime Minister,

Delegates from both countries,

Friends from media,

Namaskar!

It gives me great pleasure to extend a warm welcome to the Prime Minister of Poland in India.

During my visit to Poland in 2024, he extended a warm welcome to me and my delegation. During that visit, we elevated our relations to a Strategic Partnership.

Building on this strong foundation, our partnership has gained fresh momentum over the past two years. And in today’s meeting with the Prime Minister, we took several important decisions to further strengthen our Strategic Partnership.

Friends,

The friendship between India and Poland is rooted not only in diplomatic ties, but also in our shared heritage of humanity and compassion.

During the Second World War, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur provided refuge in India to thousands of Polish children and families. Even today, the people of Poland remember the Jam Saheb with great respect as “Dobry Maharaja,” meaning “Good Maharaja.”

In 2022, Poland carried forward this same spirit of humanity by helping ensure the safe return of our students from Ukraine. I am pleased that, through the Jam Saheb Youth Exchange Programme, young people from Poland are visiting India and carrying our historic friendship forward to the next generation.

Friends,

Today, the world is going through a period of uncertainty and change. Even in these challenging times, both India and Poland are emerging as important centres of growth, technology, and innovation.

Last year, Poland’s GDP crossed the historic milestone of one trillion dollars. I warmly congratulate Prime Minister on this achievement. Meanwhile, India also recorded an impressive growth rate of 7.8% in the last quarter.

Our growing economic strength has created new opportunities for the India-Poland partnership. The India-European Union Free Trade Agreement has further expanded these opportunities. Once the agreement comes into effect, it will open up new opportunities for India to export machinery, chemicals, plastics, and engineering goods to Poland. At the same time, we will seek new investments from Poland in sectors such as railways and mobility, advanced manufacturing, food processing, and biotechnology.

I am pleased that the Hon’ble Prime Minister has come to India with a large business delegation. We are confident that companies from both countries will work together to develop trusted supply chains for the world and achieve our shared goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.

Friends,

Today, we agreed to deepen our cooperation in defence, space, and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to partner with India in co-development and co-production.

We will also develop new partnerships in critical minerals and coal gasification, bringing together Polish expertise.

Our ties in IT and cybersecurity are already strong, with several Indian IT companies operating in Poland. Building on this cooperation, we have agreed to establish an India-Poland Startup Bridge.

These initiatives will give fresh momentum to our cooperation in AI, cybersecurity, fintech, and other emerging technologies, while creating new opportunities for the youth of both countries.

Friends,

Cultural and people-to-people ties are the greatest strength of our relationship. We are delighted that Poland has a rich tradition of Sanskrit studies and Indology.
