The manner in which India’s Captain Smita displayed patience, prudence, and courage, and as the Prime Minister of Israel said today, this Indian prevented another 9/11 from taking place. This act of valor by Smita fills every citizen of the country with pride. Today, I also spoke with his father Bhupendra Bhai, his mother Geeta Ben, and his wife Sonal. His treatment is ongoing, and today the entire world is proud of him. I appeal to the people of the country that we should all pray for Smita’s long life and excellent health, and salute our brother Smita, who has enhanced India’s glory.

Friends,

Today is not only a celebration of 100 years of the UPSC, but also a celebration of a legacy. It is a celebration of the aspirations that millions upon millions of young people cherish and pursue every year. It is a celebration of the trust that every Indian places in this institution. During this century-long journey, generations changed, governments changed, technology changed, and syllabi changed, yet the trust in the UPSC remains just as unwavering today, and that is one of your greatest assets. A commemorative postage stamp and coin marking this 100-year journey have just been released. A compilation of 100 important case laws has also been published. I pay my respects to all the distinguished individuals associated with this century-long journey. I extend my heartfelt congratulations and best wishes to all of you. A little while ago, I was visiting the gallery that has been set up here, and I would encourage all of you to spend 10 to 15 minutes exploring it. I noticed a photograph from the 75th anniversary celebrations in which Lt. General Surendra Nath can be seen. Today, at the age of 90, he is present among us.

Friends,

There are many individuals who transformed this journey into a legacy of trust, introduced changes in tune with the times, and took the institution to new heights. Every one of them deserves appreciation and recognition. While looking through the gallery, I noticed that it also contains information about how Subhas Chandra Bose went through this very process in 1920. What caught my attention was that although India was under British rule at the time, there used to be a Sanskrit paper in the examination, and Subhas Babu wrote his paper in Sanskrit.

Friends,

On this historic occasion, I would also like to pay tribute to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. After Independence, the challenge before him was not merely to keep the nation free. The challenge before him was also to govern and build a nation. The steel frame that was required for the reconstruction of the nation was provided by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. He made this institution one of the principal pillars of independent India and strengthened it.

Friends,

When the foundation of this institution was laid in 1926, the priorities of that era were different. At that time, both the focus of the system and its commitment were directed towards the British Raj. After India attained Independence, the dreams of a free India and the governance needs of a free India became the central focus. Over the past decades, the UPSC has discharged its responsibilities in an exemplary manner. Much has already been said from this stage about its achievements and contributions. Therefore, I neither wish to repeat those points nor go into detail about them. Moving beyond history, we now have India’s future waiting before us. One quarter of the 21st century, twenty-five years, has already passed. The next twenty to twenty-five years will be extremely important for India, for every citizen of India, and for every institution of India. Therefore, I would like to focus my discussion today in that direction.

Friends,

For a Developed India, the kind of governance the country now requires depends significantly on the UPSC and the State Public Service Commissions. The young people whom you are recruiting today will play a crucial role in building a Developed India, and they themselves will be among the greatest beneficiaries of a Developed India. Keeping this in mind, we must always remember two touchstones. The first touchstone is: Nation First. The second touchstone is: Citizen First. These are the two standards against which every selection must be measured. When candidates are evaluated in this spirit, and when individuals imbued with this spirit are selected, the achievement of national goals becomes far more natural and far easier.

Friends,

India in 2047 will be very different from the India of today. India will be far more urbanized than it is today. The gap between villages and cities will narrow. The aspirations and expectations of our citizens, especially our youth, will be significantly greater. The signs of this transformation are already visible. Therefore, the question today is not merely one of service delivery. The question is also whether public services are able to keep pace with the speed of today’s world of instant delivery. Are they able to move at that pace? Today, citizens do not want to wait weeks or months for a service. When AI can process thousands of documents within moments, and when governments have access to real-time data, citizens expect quick solutions. This changing mindset also demands new changes from our civil services. Therefore, we must align our selection parameters and recruitment processes with the needs of the future. We need to bring into public service those young people who are attracted not by public office, but by public service. Therefore, it is important that recruitment examinations should not merely assess how much a candidate knows. They should also assess why that young person wants to join the civil services. Because when the motivation is right, it becomes easier both to keep pace with changing public aspirations and to adapt to them.

Friends,

Many of you are familiar with the fact that whenever I meet trainee officers, I ask them to write down, right at the beginning and in their own handwriting, why they have joined the civil service. This is because responsibilities increase over time and new challenges emerge. At such moments, that small note reminds them of their original purpose. It also becomes a self-appraisal tool for them. UPSC and the State Commissions may also consider developing a similar mechanism.

Friends,

We have seen that period in the past when it was believed that the government was the ultimate guardian and provider. But today, our mantra is, “Nagrik Devo Bhava” (The Citizen is Divine). In other words, the citizen of this country is no less than a deity for us. Service to the citizen is our highest priority.

Therefore, friends,

Twenty-first-century India is moving forward with a new work culture. Its core principle is: Pro-People, Pro-Active, Good Governance! Pro-People means working not according to the convenience of the government, but by placing the interests of citizens above everything else. Pro-Active means preparing solutions by anticipating problems before they arise, instead of acting only after problems appear. Good Governance means there should be neither absence of government, nor pressure from government, nor unnecessary influence. At both the national and state levels, we must design our selection processes in accordance with this spirit. We must provide the nation with professionals who possess the sensitivity to understand the suffering of the poor; who willingly step forward with youthful energy; who find innovative solutions to difficult challenges; who understand the needs of the nation; who ensure compliance with the law; and who can also judge whether a law is making people’s lives easier or whether it is becoming an obstacle.

Friends,

We are all witnessing the rapid pace at which the times are changing and technology is evolving. The period that lies ahead is going to present society with new kinds of challenges. We are all familiar with the global debate currently taking place around AI. In such a scenario, our civil servants too will be required to work under very different circumstances. There will be situations involving information warfare, the challenge of deepfakes, concerns regarding algorithmic bias, and complex questions such as climate justice. Therefore, in our selection processes, we must also give priority to assessing complex problem-solving abilities and long-term vision, and to making deliberate efforts in that direction.

Friends,

We all know that today our nation is moving rapidly on the expressway of reforms. At such a time, our examination-conducting agencies must move quickly on reforms that are the need of the hour. One such important issue is the time taken to conduct examinations. We must not view an examination merely as an event. It is connected not only to an event but to the future and lives of young people. A delay of even a few months in examinations can become a serious challenge for them. Coaching fees, rent, transportation expenses, all of these impose a heavy burden on families. Therefore, it is extremely important that our examination system adopts the principle of time certainty. UPSC and all selection commissions across the country must ensure that, without lowering standards, we find ways to shorten our examination cycle. In fact, while I was looking at the gallery, I noticed that nearly one hundred days have already been reduced. This achievement certainly deserves appreciation, and I congratulate all of you for it.

But friends,

This is not merely an administrative reform. It is also a reform that promotes equity.

Friends,

All of you are aware of the Chief Secretaries’ Conference and the DGP Conference. Over the last ten years, these have evolved into important institutional mechanisms. Under these forums, all the Chief Secretaries of the country come together for three days to deliberate and exchange ideas. Similarly, during the DGP Conference, all the Directors General of Police gather for three days to discuss issues and share experiences. One objective of these conferences is to help one state learn about, understand, and, where appropriate, adopt the best practices of another state. I have been informed that every year UPSC organizes a National Conference in partnership with State Public Service Commissions. To make this conference broader, more productive, and richer in new ideas, I am sure you are continuously thinking about giving it a new shape and a new dimension. Such efforts help institutions share their best practices with one another. At the same time, this conference should also study international best practices. Focused discussions should also be held on how technology can be used to improve the efficiency of our processes and procedures. Such efforts at cross-learning will benefit UPSC as well as every state selection commission. We must also consider standardizing procedural norms and processes. This will provide significant assistance to young people.

Friends,

Another important subject is capacity building within UPSC and the state selection commissions. This effort should continue on a sustained basis. The iGOT platform developed under Mission Karmayogi can also be used for our internal systems, for strengthening the capabilities of our teams, and for enhancing the efficiency of our institutions through these various platforms.

Friends,

You must always remember that your work is linked directly to the future of India’s youth. In other words, you are an important pillar in the mission of transforming youth power into national power. Over the years, you have played a major role in advancing this mission. When UPSC was established, opportunities were more readily available to young people from large cities, economically privileged families, and prestigious institutions. Today, however, youth from villages and small towns are also entering public service. The participation of our daughters is also steadily increasing. In 1952, women constituted only 3 percent of candidates in the civil services, just three percent. Today that figure has risen to more than 30 percent. In the entire history of UPSC, there have been four women Chairpersons. The time for applause comes now. Out of those four women Chairpersons in UPSC’s entire history, three have been appointed after 2014. These changes are not merely statistics; they demonstrate how greatly the scope of opportunity has expanded in our country.

Friends,

In 1976, when UPSC completed fifty years, the number of candidates appearing for examinations was far lower than it is today. Compared to that period, the number of examination aspirants has increased by more than forty-five times. In other words, today we have before us an enormous pool of talent. This is a matter of immense pride for the nation. At the same time, our responsibility has grown proportionately. When we possess such a vast talent pool, one that is the envy of the world, you are not merely selecting a candidate. You are choosing an individual who will later become a representative of the government. At the grassroots level, people will regard that individual as the government itself. Therefore, all of you bear a tremendous responsibility to select the right person.

Friends,

During its first century, UPSC has continuously strengthened its credibility and earned the trust of the nation. Now, as this institution enters its second century, it must enrich and deepen that credibility in accordance with new possibilities and new challenges. While preserving the values that have been our strength until now, we must also upgrade ourselves to meet the demands of the future. UPSC’s independence, impartiality, commitment to merit, confidentiality, and fair procedures constitute its defining identity. These values must always be preserved. With this appeal, I once again extend my heartfelt congratulations and best wishes to all of you.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-address-in-the-138th-episode-of-mann:
My dear countrymen, Namaskar.

I am getting an opportunity to meet you once again for the September edition of ‘Mann Ki Baat’. I welcome all the people of the country. In ‘Mann Ki Baat’, we provide a platform for the positive efforts of our countrymen… discuss the nation’s achievements. One such major, historic achievement of India is set to mark its 10th anniversary in just a day – this achievement is the ‘Surgical Strike’. Ten years ago, on September 28-29, 2016, the Indian Army carried out surgical strikes on terrorist hideouts in Pakistan. The world was astonished to see the manner in which our brave soldiers crossed the Line of Control (LoC) to take action against terrorism.

The surgical strike boldly demonstrated to the entire world a new example of India’s counter-terrorism policy. The ‘Surgical Strike’ was our decisive response to the long-standing pain India had endured due to terrorist attacks. Over the past decade – from the Balakot airstrike to ‘Operation Sindoor’ – India has repeatedly sent a clear message: if terrorists dare to cast an evil eye on India, they will be met with a befitting response.

Friends,

India has long suffered wounds inflicted by terrorist attacks. There was a time when serial blasts had become a common occurrence in the country. It was in this very month of September – specifically on September 13, 2008 – that many innocent lives were lost in the serial blasts in Delhi. Just a few weeks later, the massive 26/11 attack took place in Mumbai. Friends, in the past too, there used to be demands for action against Pakistan following every terror attack, but such calls were often not given due attention; time to pass by was simply awaited. Today, India pursues a zero-tolerance policy against terrorism, and we are witnessing the results of that.

Friends,

This year also marks 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Among the innocent lives lost at the World Trade Center in the US, the highest number of victims—after Americans – was Indians. I recall that after becoming Prime Minister in 2014, when I visited the US, I had reached New York to pay my homage to those innocent citizens. Today, once again, I extend my condolences to the bereaved families on behalf of crores of Indian citizens.

My dear countrymen,

A grand picture of the nation is currently emerging. This picture includes you, your family and even your neighbours. I am referring to India’s census. The first phase of this exercise is nearly complete across all states and union territories;

data of over 32 crore families has already been recorded. Work is currently underway also in the remote, snow-clad regions of Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, and Uttarakhand. Many inspiring experiences have emerged from these areas. In Uttarakhand, the census process began in the village of Mana in Chamoli; Mana is known as the country’s first village. The process there started with 83-year-old Purnima Rawat ji. In Bagori village, Uttarkashi, Hardev Singh Rana ji—who runs a homestay—entered his details himself using digital means.

Friends,

The census is a national responsibility for all of us. On 15th August also, I had urged my countrymen to take time out for that. The facility to self-register your census details is very convenient. You can register information about yourself and your family from your mobile itself. Along with Hindi, this facility is available in 16 languages.

Friends,

To do this, you need to visit the census online portal. The portal is se.census.gov.in… log in using your mobile number, enter your location, fill in the details regarding your family and submit the information. The entire process takes about 15 to 20 minutes. And for that you do not need to upload any document. After submitting the information, you will receive a special ID. You can share this ID with the census enumerator when they visit your home. After the information you provided is verified, it will become part of the census record.

Friends,

So far, more than 2 crore 60 lakh people have already entered their details on the census portal via mobile – completing the self-enumeration. It will take a little of your time, but it is important for the nation, as accurate information about you and your family helps create a precise picture of the country’s future.

My dear countrymen,

Today – the date 27th of September – has become even more special for a special reason. Today marks the 100th birth anniversary of a great personality who had dedicated his entire life to culture, society, and the nation. I am speaking of the revered late Ashok Singhal ji, the former International Working President of the Vishwa Hindu Parishad. He was born on this very day – September 27, 1926 – in Agra. Living amidst society, he led life like an ascetic. The very direction and energy he imparted to the Ram Janmabhoomi movement veritably resulted in us witnessing the magnificent temple in Ayodhya today. I’ve been greatly fortunate… I’ve not only observed his life closely but also have had the opportunity to join him in this mission. It was only natural for me to be reminded of Ashok ji repeatedly while participating in the *Pran Pratishtha* ceremony at the Ram Mandir.

Friends,

There are so many aspects about Ashok ji that do not receive much attention. Alongside the Ram Mandir movement, he also waged a major battle against social discrimination and inequality. He was born into a very affluent family; his father was a civil services official, and most of his siblings held high-ranking positions. He himself was a graduate of IIT BHU. Yet, despite all that, he dedicated his life to society and culture – this is the hallmark of great individuals. Today, on the occasion of his birth centenary, I bow to him on behalf of his millions of admirers… I offer my heartfelt tribute, on my part.

My dear countrymen,

We began this year with a grand celebration of national pride – This festival was the “Somnath Swabhiman Parv”. A thousand years ago, in 1026, Mahmud of Ghazni had demolished the Somnath Temple for the first time. However, those who came to destroy Somnath and erase India’s identity have no existence at all today, whereas the Somnath Temple stands in all its grandeur by the vast sea, bestowing the blessing of immortality upon India. That is why we celebrated the ‘Somnath Swabhiman Parv’ this year with immense pride.

Friends,

Why I am bringing this up again in ‘Mann Ki Baat’ today – there is a special reason for that. In 1026 AD when Somnath was destroyed by Ghazni; the same year, the famous Sun Temple in Modhera, Gujarat, was also attacked and destroyed. This means that a thousand years have passed since the destruction of the Modhera temple as well, whereas the temple then had been built just a year ago. King Bhimdev had got it built in 1025.

Friends,

Imagine that era; a massive invasion had taken place, a major center of faith like the Somnath Temple had been vandalised, and attacks were occurring at multiple locations – any society or administration could have had its morale shattered. Yet, King Bhimdev The First not only confronted the forces of Ghazni but also had the Modhera Sun Temple rebuilt within a short time. It is because of this very resilience that the Somnath Temple, too, was rebuilt every time despite facing repeated destruction.

Friends,

The attacks on the Modhera Sun Temple did not cease in later periods either. Alauddin Khilji later destroyed this temple, the magnificent architectural marvel once again. However, friends, we, the people of India, do not worship the Sun solely through architecture and temples; for us, Sun worship also signifies light, energy, science, and the inspiration for continuity. That is why Modhera is known today not just for its Sun Temple; this village in Gujarat has become the country’s first ‘Surya Gram’ ‘Solar Village.’

Modhera now runs entirely on solar energy, setting an example of sustainability for the nation. Several attractions and amenities for tourists have also been introduced in Modhera. The Modhera Dance Festival is held there in January, following Makar Sankranti, featuring magnificent performances of India’s cultural and classical dances. I would urge all of you to visit Modhera at least once and witness this glorious Indian heritage.

Friends,

Our connection with the past remains very much alive today. This is driven by the dedication and hard work of individuals who are deepening this bond. A unique initiative of this kind is underway in Manapparai, Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu. A. Selvaraju ji, associated with the Department of Tamil Studies at a college, is spearheading this effort. During a lecture, he learned about some ancient sculptures from a student. Following a discussion on the subject, he planned a field visit. During this visit, he discovered several sculptures and ancient temples at various locations. This is a fascinating way to connect with the past; this way, we can understand our heritage even better. Similar initiatives can be undertaken in other parts of the country as well… they offer us the opportunity to observe and comprehend our history more closely.

My dear countrymen,

In just a few days, it’s the 2nd of October – the birth anniversary of revered Bapu. Bapu has given us many guiding principles for life… cleanliness is one of them. We often see numerous efforts related to cleanliness around us. These efforts are very inspiring and uplifting. Such photos, videos, and reels frequently catch our attention on social media as well. I have witnessed many such initiatives recently. At a place in Madhya Pradesh, young people are working to clean up a river; the entire community is joining in their small effort. Similarly, in Andhra Pradesh, the youth are cleaning up old stepwells and wells, thereby helping to restore our ancient heritage. In Mumbai, some young people are taking the initiative to keep beaches clean; every week, hundreds of young friends gather at one beach or the other to serve through cleanliness drives… Swachhata Se Sewa. Here in Delhi, children and the youth are raising awareness about segregating waste and maintaining cleanliness in their surroundings. In West Bengal, young students are collaborating with locals to clean up market areas at picnic spots.

Friends,

Across all these efforts, one aspect is easily observed… somewhere it starts with a single individual, other people join in, and the movement grows – this is precisely what ‘Jan-Bhagidari’ is all about. Indeed, cleanliness is the most beautiful tribute we can pay to Bapu.

My dear countrymen,

When we protect the environment, we do not merely save plants or animals; we strengthen that entire ecosystem. Some initiatives taking place in various parts of the country are beautifully highlighting this sentiment.

Friends,

There is the Sonai Rupai Wildlife Sanctuary in Assam. There was a time when elephants used to inhabit this area, but as human interference on forest land increased, the elephants moved away. Three years ago, this land was cleared of encroachment, and the results have been remarkable – the elephants have returned here again. Herds of elephants are once again being spotted in areas where they had not been active for years. Friends, another wonderful initiative has taken place in Assam itself – this effort is to save a tiny creature, the Pygmy Hog. Once, its very existence was under threat; at that time, a conservation program was launched with just six Pygmy Hogs, and they were reintroduced into the wild. Grasslands were also curated for their living. Today, thanks to this program, the Pygmy Hog population has risen to over 190.

Friends,

Our relationship with nature is not limited merely to its preservation; often, when we care for nature, it becomes a source of sustenance for our own lives. In the Sundarbans of West Bengal, some women are setting an inspiring example of this very bond. These women from Jharkhali are creating mangrove forests.

Most of them are women who lost their husbands to tiger attacks. After losing their husbands, they found a means of livelihood within the Sundarbans itself. The mangroves they have planted are now serving as a natural protective shield for their villages, while also providing them with an income. Friends, let us conserve the environment, respect the balance of nature, and safeguard its diversity. Every such effort of ours is a responsibility we owe to future generations.

My dear countrymen,

Millions of young people across the country have recently taken a significant resolve against substance abuse and drugs. They have vowed to stay away from drugs themselves and have also taken up the responsibility of spreading this message to others – all under the ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva Abhiyan’. This campaign will run for 100 weeks… it includes volunteers from ‘MY Bharat’. Our youth associated with the NSS are part of this; schools, colleges, and universities have joined in; and numerous social and spiritual organizations are also involved. In just the last few days, thousands of pledge ceremonies and awareness programs have taken place across the country. Friends, there is one aspect of this campaign that I particularly appreciate: the ‘Nasha-Mukti Ka Sandesh.’ Our youth are propagating this message in their own language and in their own way.

I had urged young people in ‘Mann Ki Baat’ as well, to join this campaign using their creativity, and I am delighted that thousands of youth have stepped forward in response to this call. Various competitions – such as anthem – slogan writing, and street plays – have been organized on the ‘MY Bharat’ platform. Similarly, young people are sharing creative content on social media using the hashtag ‘#NashaMuktYuva’; in essence, the message, the medium, and the driving energy behind it all come from the youth themselves. In the coming days, activities such as health check-ups and meditation camps will also be conducted as part of this campaign.

Friends,

Several of our festivals are approaching soon. This time amidst the festive celebrations, let us also look around us. If any young person is drifting towards a harmful habit, talk to them. If someone is trying to break free from addiction, support them. Let us all work together to advance the resolve of a drug-free youth and a Viksit Bharat.

My dear countrymen,

I announced a talent hunt campaign for sports from the Red Fort this time. To ensure India continues to perform excellently, it is essential to reach out to villages and towns to discover sporting talent. At the same time, there are many individuals who have dedicated themselves to this very cause. Their sole passion is to discover talent and shape it.

In our Punjab, Rajinder Singh ji is doing exactly this work. Rajinder Singh ji is one such individual who also carries the title ‘Senior’ as part of his name. He was part of the team that won the gold medal in hockey at the 1980 Olympics. He shone at the 1982 World Cup. In 2001, India won the Men’s Junior World Cup title for the first time, whereas in 2003, the country clinched the Senior Asia Cup title. He played the role of the coach in both these tournaments. Now, he is pursuing his passion through the Round Glass Hockey Academy. Thanks to his efforts, new hockey astro-turfs are being laid in villages. Rajinder ji has a very clear focus: identifying children in villages that lack access to excellent coaching facilities. Through such initiatives, many players are securing spots at India’s junior and senior levels. No matter how much Rajinder Singh ji’s dedication is lauded, it’s not enough.

My dear countrymen,

*Amla*, the Indian gooseberry is very familiar to all of us. Pickles and preserves i.e. *murabba* made from it are used in most households. Many people like *Amla* juice and *Chyawanprash* becomes an essential part of our daily routine during winter. Our elders have long spoken about the qualities of *Amla* across generations. Friends, this very *Amla* is now becoming a source of new possibilities in Pratapgarh, Uttar Pradesh. The bond between Pratapgarh and *Amla* is very old; farmers here have been growing it for generations.

*Amla* has given Pratapgarh a strong identity, and now, this long-standing identity is bringing new opportunities for local farmers and women. The ‘One District One Product’ (ODOP) has boosted local entrepreneurs involved in the *Amla* trade there. Today, around 100 units related to *Amla* processing are operational in Pratapgarh, with women connected with self-help groups playing a significant role. One such group is from Devgarh Kamasi village; women associated with the Savitri Phule Self-Help Group are producing *Amla* candy, preserves, and juice. Access to new markets through the ODOP scheme has also led to an increase in their income.

Similarly, there is a ‘Vindhyavasini Self-Help Group’ in a village. The women of this group are producing many such items like Amla pickle and digestive powder. These women received machinery for processing and access to loan facilities. They also got the opportunity to participate in local trade fairs, and in no time, their income saw a significant rise.

Friends,

Every region of our country certainly possesses some such unique specialty – be it a specific fruit, a traditional art form, or a unique skill. The ‘One District, One Product’ campaign aims to promote these very specialties.

Our endeavour should be to ensure that the identity of our villages and small towns is not confined merely to local markets; these products should reach other parts of the country and even global markets. This also strengthens the ‘Vocal for Local’ campaign… it inspires the nation to become self-reliant. Even during the upcoming festive season, we must never forget the ‘Vocal for Local’ mantra.

My dear countrymen,

The month of September is dedicated to the fight against malnutrition. During the Nutrition Month, individuals and organizations from various sectors come together for this noble cause.

Several commendable initiatives have been launched this year to combat malnutrition. Chhattisgarh, for instance, has started the ‘Har Ghar Munga – Ghar Ghar Munga’ campaign… through this, people are being encouraged to include the nutritious *Munga* i.e. Moringa in their diet. Gujarat has also launched a ‘Vangi Spardha’ – a competition featuring dishes made from millets. This initiative promotes affordable and nutritious local cuisine. So far, more than two lakh people have participated in this contest. Maharashtra is also making commendable efforts in this direction; teachers, Anganwadi workers, and parents are joining awareness campaigns there. In Mizoram as well, people have come together this year to launch a campaign for the upkeep of ‘Poshan Vatikas’. This aligns with the Mizo tradition of ‘Talo-Mad-Yana,’ which signifies selfless service and always being at the forefront of helping others.

Such efforts are truly praiseworthy. I am also proud of everyone associated with Anganwadi centres who has been part of such initiatives. These Anganwadi centres are now digitally connected via the ‘Poshan Tracker,’ with approximately nine crore beneficiaries registered on the platform. This has enabled better care for children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers. We must continue this fight against malnutrition with the same spirit; we have to make our society completely free from malnutrition.

Friends,

All of us have celebrated Ganesha Utsav this month with great devotion and enthusiasm. Ganpati Bappa was welcomed across the country with deep reverence. This sacred occasion fills the entire atmosphere with joy and exuberance. Friends, Vighnharta Bhagwan Shri Ganesha symbolizes knowledge, wisdom, and the auspicious beginning of any endeavour. Deep reverence for Him exists not only in India; take the example of Shriman Panthoun Thirkhanon ji – he hails from Thailand. There, Lord Shri Ganesha is worshipped as ‘Phra Phikanet.’ When he was 19 years old, his father gifted him a photograph of Bhagwan Shri Ganesha. It was then that a profound sense of devotion awakened within him. He has spent over four decades studying traditions associated with Bhagwan Shri Ganesha. He has travelled across several Asian countries, including India and Nepal. He has held a special affection for Maharashtra.

After learning about the *Ashtavinayak* tradition, he has visited the region numerous times. Through his efforts, the *Ashtavinayak* yatra has gained popularity among devotees in Thailand as well. In 2002, he established the Ganesha Himal Museum in Chiang Mai, northern Thailand. Today, it houses more than 10,000 idols of Ganesha. The museum also has *Ashtavinayak* idols for devotees who are unable to travel to India. Worship rituals for Ganesha ji are conducted here every Sunday morning around 10 o’clock. Also, on special occasions connected with Ganesha, celebrations are held. This demonstrates how India’s faith, art, and cultural traditions are gaining popularity in other countries as well. I wish that the blessings of Ganpati Bappa remain with everyone always.

Friends,

After every episode of ‘Mann Ki Baat,’ I receive messages from you on myriad topics. Do continue to share such inspiring stories. When you appreciate the initiatives taking place around you, the enthusiasm of those involved grows even further. Learning about these efforts through ‘Mann Ki Baat’ inspires people in other parts of the country as well. May this journey continue to move forward with your support. Celebrate the upcoming festivals with great joy and enthusiasm with your family and friends. I extend my best wishes to all of you once again.

Thank you very much.

Namaskar.
texts.pms-remarks-during-20th-rozgar-mela-via-:
My dear young companions,

The festive season has begun in the country. Amidst these celebrations, today brings a new joy into the lives of thousands of families. Today, more than 51,000 youth across the nation are receiving appointment letters for government service. Behind the achievement you have reached today is not only your hard work, but also the dedication of your parents and family members. I extend heartfelt congratulations to all of you and your families. I wish you all the best for this new beginning in life.

Friends,

Today you are joining the Government of India at a time when the nation is moving towards a very big goal – the goal of making India developed by 2047. In this, the role of youth like you is immense. While serving in government, you must take every decision that strengthens the campaign for a developed India and for self‑reliant India. As youth, you have a special responsibility towards other young people. You can see how the talent and skills of our youth have won the trust of the entire world. The world has great expectations from our innovators, entrepreneurs, and youth power. Just a few days ago, the BRICS Summit concluded. India’s effort has been that BRICS cooperation should not remain limited to governments alone – our entrepreneurs, farmers, women, youth, everyone should become active participants in this partnership. With this vision, initiatives like BRICS CONNECT and the BRICS MSME Cooperation Portal have been launched.

Friends,

In recent years, India has signed free trade agreements with nearly 40 countries. These FTAs are opening new doors of opportunity for our youth. Such trade agreements create new partnerships for our entrepreneurs, open new markets, and create new career possibilities for our youth.

Friends,

In recent years, the Government of India has consistently focused on preparing youth for the future. The National Education Policy, Skill India Mission, Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, and efforts to promote apprenticeships – all aim to ensure that the education and skills of our youth align with the needs of a changing economy. One example is PM‑SETU. Through this scheme, with an investment of 60,000 crore rupees, 1,000 government ITIs are being modernized. Direct participation of industry has been ensured in this.

Friends,

Another picture of the strength of India’s youth is visible in our startup ecosystem. Today India is the world’s third‑largest startup ecosystem. And India’s startup story is no longer just about big cities. Today, nearly half of recognized startups are in tier‑two and tier‑three cities. That means youth from villages, towns, and small cities are also playing a big role in India’s new economy. Our young people from smaller towns are working on their ideas, building new companies, and creating new employment opportunities for other youth as well.

Friends,

Our effort is that new employment opportunities also grow rapidly in the private sector. With this vision, the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana has been launched. About 1 lakh crore rupees are being spent on this scheme. With its help, nearly 20 million youth will get the chance to join the workforce for the first time. Under this scheme, the government is giving an incentive of up to 15,000 rupees to youth who get their first job. Employers who create new jobs are also being encouraged by the government. That means the government is working on every front to increase employment in the country.

Friends,

New opportunities for youth are created only when the country’s economy grows, when investment increases, new industries are set up, and new sectors expand. Today India is one of the fastest‑growing major economies. In the first quarter of this financial year, India’s growth rate was 7.8 percent. Investment increased by nearly 12 percent. Rating agencies are upgrading India’s ratings. And this progress is happening at a time when the world is passing through many uncertainties. Behind India’s growth is the major contribution of reforms carried out in recent years. In your tenure, you must continue to accelerate reforms. Whether it is simplifying tax and compliance, increasing ease of doing business, reforms in education and skilling, opening new sectors for innovation, or ease of living – at every level, the Reform Express must continue at full speed. And as government employees, you will have a very big role in this in the present and coming years.

Friends,

I said a few days ago – the sun must be ours, the sea must be ours. The boat must be ours, the sailor must be ours. The courage to write victory on the waves must be ours. Today India’s youth are moving forward with this courage. Now, while serving in the Government of India, it is your responsibility to understand the aspirations of the country’s youth and fulfill your duties accordingly. I urge you again – every decision you take, every signature you put on a file, must advance the aspirations of youth. In your tenure, you must ensure that obstacles in the path of youth are removed, their ideas get opportunities to move forward, innovation increases investment, and investment creates new employment opportunities.

Friends,

Now you are becoming part of the government system yourselves. Therefore, your effort must be that the difficulties you faced, or that your parents faced, should not be faced by other youth. The hardships your parents endured, the hardships you may have endured – no citizen of our country should have to endure them anymore. This is the work you must do as soon as you enter the government system.

Friends,

Today, transformation is happening rapidly in every sector of the country. You have reached here by continuously learning. Now from here begins a new journey of continuous learning. You must keep improving your skills. You must understand new technologies and new systems. Mission Karmayogi helps you achieve this very purpose. More than 17 million government employees are connected to the iGOT Karmayogi platform today. And for new companions like you, Karmayogi Prarambh has been specially designed. The more you improve yourself, the better you will serve the citizens of the country.

Friends,

You must always remember one more thing. The real strength of government is the trust of the country’s citizens. Whatever ministry you are in, whatever department you are in, your work will touch the life of ordinary citizens in some way. A pension for an elderly person may move forward because of your work. A scholarship for a student may depend on your responsibility. A facility for a farmer may be delivered through your department. For some citizen, you may be the face of the government. Your behavior, your sensitivity, your efficiency, your honesty – all these will determine how that citizen experiences the government.

Therefore, friends,

In government service, our mantra must be – Citizen Devo Bhava, Citizen Devo Bhava. Service to citizens is service to the nation. Your success will be greater when your work makes life easier for a citizen. I am confident that wherever you are, in whichever department you are, you will continue to fulfill your duties with dedication and a spirit of service. Once again, I congratulate you all.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-address-at-the-international-confere:
Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant ji, my colleague in the Union Cabinet Bhupender Yadav ji, Attorney General of India R. Venkataramani ji, National Green Tribunal (NGT) Chairman Justice Prakash Srivastava ji, all distinguished dignitaries present in this hall, ladies and gentlemen.

For centuries, India has guided the world on the subject of nature and environment. With that ideological commitment, and based on our cultural experiences, India is now also providing solutions to modern climate challenges, while at the same time calling for collective efforts of humanity. I am happy that this NGT conference is carrying forward that mission. For this event, I extend my congratulations and best wishes to all the officials of NGT and all dignitaries associated with it.

Friends,

We all know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions has been wrongly placed on developing countries. Many of my companions from the Global South are present here. But the historical truth is that even today, India’s per capita carbon emissions are less than half the global average. In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than India’s. Six times higher. India presents this fact strongly on global platforms. And I say to every Indian – show your strength too. We have also presented our traditions and their power before the world. On these very subjects, during COP‑21 in Paris, we launched the book Convenient Action – Continuity for Change. We are establishing new benchmarks for environmental protection by taking the world along. Whether it is the vision of One Sun, One World, One Grid, or the International Solar Alliance, CDRI, Global Biofuel Alliance, International Big Cat Alliance, Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) – each of these platforms is becoming a stage for India’s dedicated commitments on climate and environment.

Friends,

Today’s India is moving forward by weaving its ancient ideas of environmental protection into a modern vision. In the past 12 years, India has made extraordinary progress in every sector related to the environment. Our major focus has been on renewable energy, and this has played a big role in environmental protection. India is the only country in the G20 – I say this before the big leaders of the G20 – the only country that has fulfilled all the commitments it made at the COP‑21 summit in Paris, and has done so ahead of schedule. This is the strength of Hindustan that I am talking about. On every parameter – non‑fossil fuel, solar energy capacity, curbing carbon emissions – India’s performance is today a subject of positive discussion worldwide. Look at the figures. Twelve years ago, India’s solar energy capacity was about 2 gigawatts. Twelve years ago – 2 gigawatts. If there are lawyers here, please note these figures, they may come in handy. Today it has crossed 160 gigawatts. From 2 gigawatts to 160 gigawatts in 12 years. Under the PM Surya Ghar Free Electricity Scheme, we launched the mission to make homes themselves centers of solar power generation. Under this scheme, more than 5 million homes have already installed rooftop solar panels. This is more than the total number of homes in many countries. For this, the government has provided financial assistance of up to 80,000 rupees per household. Under the KUSUM scheme, the government has installed solar pumps in the fields of 3 million farmers. We have also completed the ambitious One Nation, One Grid project. Not only this – LED bulbs in homes have proven successful in saving electricity. Crores of LED bulbs have been distributed to households. And the results of these efforts are before us today. From solar energy alone, India has succeeded in preventing nearly 200 million tonnes of carbon emissions.

Friends,

Along with solar energy, India has also achieved major accomplishments in other clean energy sectors. In the past 12 years, the country’s wind energy capacity has tripled. Hydropower capacity has increased significantly. And now the country is working rapidly on nuclear energy generation. Those who give long speeches on the environment – when I advance nuclear energy work, they will stand in the courts to stop it. A pathway has also been created to bring private players into this sector. Because of these efforts, today India’s non‑fossil energy capacity has nearly quadrupled. India is also promoting technologies like coal gasification for cleaner use of coal.

Friends,

India is now working rapidly in areas like clean mobility and green hydrogen. Just a few days ago, India’s first hydrogen train was launched – and it is the world’s longest hydrogen train. This marks the beginning of a new era of clean mobility.

Friends,

In 12 years, the number of electric vehicles in our country has increased nearly 950 times. 950 times. In the year before 2014, fewer than 3,000 EVs were sold in India. Last year, nearly 2.5 million EVs were sold in India. That means India is embracing the opportunity of the EV revolution with full strength, and this is also helping the environment. On our highways and expressways, modern fast‑track systems have reduced waiting at toll booths. This has stopped the fuel wastage that used to occur at toll booths.

Friends,

Until 2014, in five cities of our country there was less than 250 kilometers of metro network. Lawyers here should note this figure. Before 2014, only five cities had less than 250 kilometers. Today, metros run in more than 20 cities, and India has joined the countries with more than 1,000 kilometers of metro network.

Friends,

With nearly 100 percent electrification of railways, billions of liters of diesel burning has been avoided. The environment has been protected. Just this month, a 3,000‑kilometer‑long Dedicated Freight Corridor was inaugurated. Every train running on it carries loads equal to hundreds of trucks from one place to another. The operation of double‑stack container freight trains is historic in itself. You can imagine how greatly this helps the environment.

Friends,

Today, transportation is happening on about 5,000 kilometers of waterways in the country. This is the most environment‑friendly mobility. A standard inland vessel running on these waterways carries loads equal to dozens of trucks in one journey. This too is greatly helping environmental protection.

Friends,

All these changes in the mobility sector alone are proof that our development is both speedy and sustainable.

Friends,

Today, with the participation of millions of people, unprecedented work is happening in India on water conservation. I am happy that more than 70,000 Amrit Sarovars have been constructed in the country. Under the Catch the Rain campaign, nearly 15 million water harvesting structures have been built, preserving rainwater. Through the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana, more than 20 million farmers today are connected with modern irrigation facilities. Initiatives like Per Drop More Crop are also saving water. Shri Anna – that is, millets – are another great successful example. India is promoting the cultivation of millets, which consume less water. In recent years, millet production has increased in the country, and exports have risen to about 150,000 tonnes. This is creating new opportunities for farmers, while also saving water. And because of this model, the world is joining us. Thanks to India’s efforts, 2023 was celebrated as the International Year of Millets.

Friends,

Under the National Mission on Natural Farming, today about 1.25 million hectares in the country have developed 24,000 clusters of natural farming. Not only this, nearly 3,000 varieties of climate‑resilient crops have also been developed in the country. By promoting agro‑forestry, we are also reducing carbon footprints.

Friends,

How wide‑ranging our efforts are can be seen in India’s forest coverage. This too I mention for my lawyer friends. In the past 12 years, our very dense forest cover has increased by more than 22 percent. This is a very big achievement. Under the campaign Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam (One Tree in the Name of Mother), crores of trees have been planted across the country. And this campaign continues.

Friends,

Plastic waste has also been a major challenge for the environment. That is why India has banned single‑use plastic. With the mantra of reduce, reuse, and recycle, we have promoted the circular economy. Today, thousands of tonnes of waste are being recycled every day in India. Through the Gobardhan Yojana, cow dung and other organic waste in villages are being converted into useful resources. Our effort is that waste should not be seen as a problem, but transformed into a resource under the Waste to Wealth model.

Friends,

All these figures are not just India’s development statistics – they are India’s contributions for the future of humanity.

Friends,

Our cultural thought is – “Mata bhumih, putro aham prithivyah” – meaning, this earth is our mother and we are her children. With this thinking, India is working to build a responsible and sustainable future. I am confident that the discussions in this conference, and the new ideas and solutions that emerge from it, may become a great support for future generations. Once again, I extend my many best wishes to all of you for this conference. Thank you very much.
texts.pms-remarks-during-the-release-of-instal:
Namaskar.

My respectful greetings and regards to all mothers of Bengal!

On this special occasion, I feel immense happiness to be connected with you. I have always received great affection from the mothers and sisters of Bengal. Your trust and warmth are a great source of strength for me.

Today is also the sacred occasion of Vishwakarma Puja. I extend my heartfelt wishes to all of you on Vishwakarma Puja.

Friends,

At this auspicious time, a new tradition is being strengthened in Bengal. Today, through the Annapurna Yojana, new empowerment is being connected with the mothers and sisters of Bengal. I congratulate and send my best wishes to every sister who is benefitting from this scheme.

Friends,

In our homes, mothers and sisters carry many responsibilities. Amidst numerous small and big decisions, a woman takes care of the family in every way. And when she has less worry about essential expenses, her confidence increases even more. The Annapurna Yojana is such an important effort to strengthen the confidence of Bengal’s women. Every month, a fixed amount reaches the bank accounts of Bengal’s sisters – an amount for which they do not have to ask anyone. This is a great support in their lives.

Friends,

Today, the fourth installment of the Annapurna Yojana is reaching the accounts of nearly 15 million sisters. That means 3,000 rupees every month. For a mother, this could be the expense of her child’s education. For a sister, it could be support for medicine or essential household items.

Friends,

Our vision is that Bengal’s women should have the power to make decisions and the courage to move forward. Annapurna Yojana plays a big role in this. I extend heartfelt congratulations to all mothers and sisters who are beneficiaries of the Annapurna Yojana.

Friends,

On May 4th this year, Bengal chose a new path of transformation. And I know, in this transformation, the most important role has been played by the mothers and sisters of Bengal. You have seen many hardships in your lives. You have waited for many things. Therefore, the first test before our new government was to make the lives of Bengal’s women easier, to increase ease of living in their lives. That is why the guiding mantra we adopted was – Less talk, more work.

Friends,

The Annapurna Yojana began with this very thought. Within just a few days of forming the government, work started on this scheme. And today, money is directly reaching the bank accounts of such a large number of women. No cut money, no middlemen!

Our government’s goal is that not a single eligible woman should be deprived of the benefits of the Annapurna Yojana. Work is progressing rapidly for this too.

Friends,

Solving every problem connected with the life cycle of mothers, sisters, and daughters has been the highest priority of the BJP. To ensure nutritious food for the child during pregnancy, we launched the Matru Vandana Yojana, sending money directly to women’s bank accounts. To prevent daughters from being eliminated in the womb, we started mass movements like Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao. To ensure daughters do not drop out of school due to lack of toilets, we built millions of toilets. To continue their education, we offered high interest in the Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana. To allow daughters to enter Sainik Schools, we opened their doors. To help daughters start their own work, we launched the Mudra Yojana with collateral‑free loans. To ensure mothers could continue their jobs after childbirth, we increased maternity leave. To provide new earning opportunities in villages, we gave record support to self‑help groups. To free daughters from smoke in the kitchen, we gave Ujjwala gas connections. To free them from the struggle of fetching water, we launched the Har Ghar Nal Se Jal scheme. To free them from darkness, we gave free electricity connections under the Saubhagya scheme. To ensure daughters do not hide their illness due to lack of money, we gave them the strength of the Ayushman card. To give daughters access to banks, we opened millions of accounts under Jan Dhan Yojana. To give daughters rights over property, we ensured joint ownership in PM Awas houses.

Friends,

One of Bengal’s great pains has been that in the past 12 years, many central schemes did not reach here on time. Poor families suffered the most because of this. Now, under the BJP government, these stalled schemes are being advanced rapidly. For example, the PM Awas Yojana. After the BJP government was formed in Bengal, more than 5 million new poor families have been identified to receive permanent houses under PM Awas. The PM Vishwakarma Yojana has also been implemented here. Every pending scheme, every stuck project, is now gaining new speed in Bengal. And in this, the blessings of Bengal’s women and people are with the BJP. That is why I say with great confidence – Together we will build a new Bengal.

Friends,

The nation has taken a pledge for a developed India. I am confident that Bengal’s mothers and sisters will continue to give new momentum to this journey of development. With the strength of a developed Bengal, the pledge of a developed India will become even stronger.

Friends,

Your affection, your blessings, continuously inspire us to serve. Once again, I extend many congratulations to all of you on Annapurna Day. Heartfelt wishes for Vishwakarma Puja! Thank you!
texts.pms-speech-during-the-inauguration-of-se:
Thank you very much.

Union Cabinet colleagues Ashwini Vaishnaw ji, Jitin Prasada ji, all industry leaders, CEOs, delegates, and virtually connected hundreds of universities and institutes – the future of India, my young companions. And here present, the large number of enthusiastic youth, ladies and gentlemen!

This is the fifth edition of Semicon India. I welcome you all. I extend a special welcome to the guests who have come from abroad.

Friends,

Today is also Vishwakarma Jayanti. I extend my best wishes to all countrymen on Vishwakarma Jayanti. In our tradition, Lord Vishwakarma is considered the symbol of the power of construction and creation. And see the coincidence – Semicon India begins today itself. On one side, our centuries‑old tradition of creation, and on the other side, the technology and vision of the 21st century – this is our inspiration for self‑reliant India, for developed India.

Friends,

Every citizen is committed to building a developed India. If we look at just the past 15 days – I draw your attention only to 15 days – we can see the direction and speed with which India is moving forward. In this September, just 10 days ago, the Global Fintech Fest was held in Mumbai. There was discussion on inclusive finance through agentic AI, tokenization, and quantum technologies. During the same period, nearly 3,000 kilometers of Dedicated Freight Corridor became fully operational in India. I am talking about September’s 10 days, not long ago. This will speed up freight movement in the country, improve logistics, and give new strength to manufacturing.

Friends,

In this same period, in this September itself, India’s quarterly GDP report came. And even in this challenging period, India achieved 7.8 percent growth. And during the same time, Japan’s credit rating agency upgraded India’s sovereign rating. And this happened after three decades – nearly 35 years. That means, on one side India’s economy is growing, and on the other side, the world’s trust in India is also increasing.

Friends,

Another big picture of this trust was seen just three days ago at the BRICS Summit. India successfully hosted this summit. The unanimous adoption of the New Delhi Declaration is another big proof of the world’s trust in India.

Friends,

Amidst these achievements of India, this Semicon India event has become even more important. Its first edition was in 2022. Since then we meet every year, but every year the subject of our discussion has changed. In the first edition, we talked about policy. In the next editions, the discussion moved forward. We began talking about projects – from signing files to laying foundation stones. Last year we began discussing pilot lines and test chips. How the first samples began to come out of India’s units – this was discussed. And this year, we are talking about commercial production. Now chips are coming out of India’s plants and reaching customers in India and the world. And just now, in Mohali and Surat, commercial production has started in two more plants. I congratulate them as well.

Friends,

For any country, reaching here in such a short time is not easy. This is not a sector where you set up a factory and the work is done. It takes decades to build technological capabilities. Wherever semiconductor ecosystems have been built in the world, they have been prepared after decades of effort. But India, with your cooperation, has worked simultaneously on chip design, manufacturing, equipment manufacturing, materials ecosystem, testing capability – and has shown success. In this journey, you industry leaders have been the major stakeholders. You are the pillars of India’s success, you are the partners in our journey.

Friends,

In the semiconductor industry, there is a word – “tape‑out.” This is the day when a chip, after design completion, goes into production. But work does not stop after tape‑out. On that very day, work begins on the next version. And India is doing the same. India has started the second phase of the Semiconductor Mission. The size of our first phase was about 8 billion dollars, while the second phase we have set at 13.5 billion dollars. Moving on the Reform Express, we have made further reforms in this sector. Now international companies can also collaborate with our startups, Indian design companies, and OCI‑owned companies. That means whether it is policies, funds, regulatory frameworks – whatever is needed for the success of your projects, the Government of India is taking every step.

Friends,

Our effort is that fabless companies grow in India, and intellectual property creation also happens in India. Whether it is making different types of compound semiconductors, making silicon photonics part of the ecosystem, or enabling infrastructure for AI – all this is necessary. And in this direction, we must move forward together. The foundation needed for this has already been prepared. India is also focusing greatly on strengthening supply chains. Many reforms have been made for this. To the leaders of equipment companies present here, I say – do not lag behind in taking advantage of this. For leaders in chemicals, gases, and materials too, golden opportunities await in India. We want the entire ecosystem to grow together. For this, the demand pipeline is also ready. So far, 12 projects have been approved, and in the next phase this scope will expand further.

Friends,

Another advantage for all of you in India is youth – talented, skilled manpower. Today we have a very large pool of engineering talent. India has thousands of engineering colleges, and every year India produces lakhs of engineers. Once, a gentleman from an American company came to meet me. He said, “If we want to recruit engineers in our country, we call them, and they all fit in one room. But in India, if we call engineers, even a football field is too small.” This is India’s strength.

And Friends,

For chip designing, large‑scale skilling work is underway. Just before coming here, I met some young companions from industry on this very campus – all students. These students gifted me chips they had designed themselves. Our government has set a target to train one lakh engineering students for the semiconductor industry. And as you were told, we have already trained more than 70,000 youth. Such a large talent pool is nothing less than a gold mine for all of you.

Friends,

Amidst these government efforts, today I also appeal to the youth – young talents who are doing research in India should come forward. Those youth who are doing research abroad should also connect with the development of advanced technologies in India. I urge industry leaders to lead R&D in the country. This benefits industry, and it also strengthens India’s youth power.

Friends,

The advancing semiconductor industry also faces some challenges, which you are all familiar with. For years, people in your industry talked about transistor size. As transistors became smaller, computing became faster and more efficient. Even today this question is important. But now, with the arrival of Artificial Intelligence, some new questions have arisen before this industry. In the past two years, the global semiconductor market has grown by more than 20 percent. And a very big part of this growth is due to demand created by AI. That means, today if you are working on AI, the challenges are not only about what is inside the chip, but also about what is happening around it. Bringing memory closer to the processor, connecting many chips in such a way that they work together as one system, transferring huge amounts of data from here to there without delay, managing heat and power – these are many challenges before the semiconductor industry. Amidst these challenges, the world most needs new and reliable manufacturing locations. And India – I assure you – India is continuously preparing itself for this.

Friends,

Another major issue before today’s semiconductor industry is energy security. The chips being made for AI are used in AI data centers. In these data centers, thousands of high‑performance processors work together, processing huge amounts of data. As AI expands, the need for computing power will increase at the same pace. And as computing power increases, the need for electricity will also increase greatly. Therefore, investment in the power sector is very important. Where our plants are located, electricity must be available on time, in the required quantity when needed – this is very important. That is why India is making very large investments in the power sector today. In the past decade, our installed solar energy capacity has increased from about 2 gigawatts to more than 160 gigawatts – from 2 to 160. In nuclear energy too, we are moving forward rapidly. This sector has been opened to private players. We are also working on small modular reactors. In the past decade, India has also expanded its transmission network.

Friends,

This expansion of power infrastructure in India is also a great strength for our semiconductor ecosystem. India is taking every step needed to make itself a preferred destination for the semiconductor industry.

Friends,

India is the Mother of Democracy. Just a few years ago, our Constitution completed 75 years. When such a country succeeds in a critical industry, it strengthens the entire world’s supply chain. And today, when supply chains are being weaponized, its importance increases even more. We must see the developments happening in India from this larger perspective. India’s aspirations are before you, and the new opportunities being created in India are ready to welcome you. Once again, I extend many congratulations to all of you for this event.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-opening-address-during-the-18th-bric:
Your Highness, Excellencies, Namaskar!

I extend a warm welcome to all of you to the extended family of BRICS.

Today, this hall brings together continents, cultures, and diverse development journeys. It is a testament to the growing strength, appeal, and unprecedented trust in BRICS.

Friends,

Under India’s Presidency, we have focused all our efforts on these four pillars: Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability. I am pleased that, with all your cooperation and support, we have been able to translate our shared vision into win-win cooperation.

Today, the number of conflicts and tensions in the world is continuously increasing, and this is having an increasingly negative and far-reaching impact on the lives of ordinary people.

Pandemics, climate disasters, and supply-chain disruptions have shown that in today’s interconnected world, no crisis remains confined to a single region. Therefore, within the BRICS group, we have placed special emphasis on strengthening Resilience. It is equally important to identify challenges in time, be prepared for them, and take prompt action.

With this approach, we have agreed on a BRICS Integrated Early Warning System for the prevention of and response to infectious diseases. Early Warning Data Integration Guidelines have been prepared for disaster management. The BRICS Logistics Supply Chain Cooperation Framework will help make our supply chains more reliable and resilient.

Friends,

Under Innovation, the BRICS Incubator Network will connect our start-ups and incubators with one another. To promote innovative and scalable solutions, we have proposed the BRICS Startup Innovation Fund.

The BRICS Network on Digital Agriculture will create new opportunities for farmers. Through this initiative, AI, geospatial technology, and Digital Public Infrastructure will be connected to the real needs of farmers.

The weaponization of technology and critical minerals can hinder our shared progress. Therefore, we have emphasised inclusivity in the adoption of technology.

Friends,

India has advanced friendship, partnership, and cooperation through the BRICS platform.

Our endeavour has been to ensure that BRICS cooperation does not remain limited to governments alone. We have sought to make our entrepreneurs, farmers, researchers, women, youth, and ordinary citizens active participants in it.

Through BRICS CONNECT, we have promoted skills, employability, women in the workforce, social security, and capacity building.

To connect small enterprises with knowledge, finance, and new markets, we have initiated the BRICS MSME Cooperation Portal.

The BRICS Urban Mobility Hub has been established to facilitate the sharing of best practices among our cities.

Friends,

In Indian civilisation, nature has been accorded the status of a mother. For centuries, we have believed that development and the environment are not alternatives to each other, but are complementary. Within BRICS as well, we have emphasised the need to strike a balance between human development and the environment.

This is the foundation of Sustainability. It is also our responsibility towards future generations. In this direction, we have made progress on several fronts.

For Smart Grids and Energy Storage, we have established the BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence. This will help make our clean energy systems more reliable, efficient, and accessible.

The Centres of Excellence for Agro-Ecology and Regenerative Agriculture will connect traditional knowledge with modern science. The principles developed for community-based climate adaptation will make indigenous knowledge an important foundation for climate action.

Friends,

Building on these four pillars, through BRICS we have sought to promote inclusive global growth. We believe that the benefits of solutions developed within BRICS should not remain confined to BRICS alone. They should be made adaptable and accessible to meet the needs of the Global South.

Friends,

From my personal experience, I can say that the Global South countries’ confidence in BRICS has grown, because within BRICS:

Their voices are heard. Their experiences are respected. And solutions are developed not for them, but together with them.

The strength of BRICS lies in our diversity and cooperation.

We may be rooted in different realities, but together, we rise through cooperation, and blossom for humanity.

May our diversity remain our identity, our cooperation become our inspiration, and our progress serve the cause of all humanity.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-opening-remarks-during-the-18th-bric:
Your Highness, Excellencies, Namaskar!

It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India.

India’s BRICS Chairship is guided by a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability have been our key priorities. With these priorities in mind, we have placed special emphasis on making BRICS cooperation more closely connected with the lives of ordinary people.

With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams in nearly 30 cities across India. I sincerely thank each one of you for your active contribution and support in making India’s BRICS Chairship a success.

Friends,

This year’s BRICS Summit marks a historic milestone. We are celebrating the 20th anniversary of BRICS. In human life, the age of twenty marks the beginning of a new phase of maturity and responsibility. It is a stage when dreams are accompanied by responsibilities, and capabilities are channelled in new directions.

Today, BRICS too stands at a ‘coming of age’ moment. Over the past twenty years, BRICS has established a distinct identity for itself on the global stage. We respect each other’s perspectives and move forward through consensus. We strive to move ahead with an approach that is not against anyone but instead seeks to take everyone along.

It is now time for us to translate our unity and consensus within BRICS into concrete outcomes on the global stage. For the next twenty years, we must work on a new and ambitious agenda. We must begin by strengthening our own working systems.

The BRICS Chairship changes every year, but this should not interrupt our institutional momentum. I propose the establishment of a BRICS Continuity and Implementation Mechanism. Through the Troika, this mechanism will ensure systematic follow-up on all initiatives and outcomes.

We can create a secure digital repository in which, for every decision, the nodal point, timeline, and implementation status can be recorded.

Friends,

While strengthening BRICS, we must also chart the course for global reform. The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid. At the top, power and decision-making are concentrated, while at the bottom are countries that are affected by these decisions but have little say in shaping them.

The Global South is today in the front row of global crises, but in the back row of decision-making. We must transform this “pyramid of privilege” into a “platform of partnership”, where every country has a voice, every member has a stake, and the advancement of humanity remains at the heart of every endeavour.

With this objective, I propose that we work together to formulate ten proposals for global governance reform, which we could seek to develop into a BRICS Reform Roadmap by the next Summit.

In preparing this roadmap, we must keep three key aspects in mind: Representation, Responsiveness, and Rule-making.

First, with regard to Representation, I would like to say that reform of the UN Security Council can no longer be delayed. The text-based negotiations on this issue must be linked to a clearly defined timeline and concrete outcomes.

Similarly, in financial institutions, voting power, leadership positions, and policy priorities should reflect today’s economic realities. Countries that drive global economic growth should also have an appropriate role in shaping global economic governance.

Second, Responsiveness. Global institutions will earn the trust of humanity only when they are able to provide effective solutions to global challenges. We must focus on the speed, scale, and last-mile impact of our collective response.

Seafarers make a very significant contribution to global trade, yet they often find themselves without adequate support during times of difficulty. I propose whether we can establish a Seafarers Emergency Support Network? This network could connect the Maritime authorities and missions of the countries concerned. It could facilitate distress alerts, medical assistance, communication with families, and support for evacuation.

And third, I would like to speak about rule-making. Ensuring equal participation in shaping the global rules of the future is of utmost importance.

AI, cyberspace, outer space, biotechnology, and critical technologies are shaping not only the opportunities of the future, but also the rules that will govern the future.

We must work to transform the Global South from rule-takers into rule-shapers. Through BRICS, we can provide young diplomats and policymakers from the countries of the Global South with negotiation skills, practical training, and legal expertise.

By a happy coincidence, today is the United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation. It is especially significant that such a decision is being taken on a day dedicated to the Global South. India is ready to take the lead on this issue.

Friends,

The message of the BRICS Summit being hosted by India should be loud and clear: If our future is shared, then the right to shape that future must also be shared.

From voice to impact. From privilege to partnership.

This should be the resolve of BRICS at 20.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-address-at-the-brics-business-forum-:
Excellencies Leaders of the BRICS business community, Innovators and friends, Namaskar!

A warm welcome to all of you to the BRICS Business Forum.

This year, we are celebrating twenty years of BRICS. When the group was launched in 2006, it comprised only four countries. Today, including BRICS and its partners, we have a family of twenty-one countries.

Today, the BRICS countries represent 50% of the world’s population, 40% of global GDP, and more than 25% of global trade. Not only that, over these years, while global GDP has grown by around 2.5 times, the combined GDP of BRICS countries has grown by around 4.5 times. In other words, the economic strength of BRICS has grown at nearly twice the pace of the world economy.

BRICS countries are also emerging as important centres for global innovation and solutions. From grassroots initiatives to frontier technologies, new possibilities for innovation are taking shape across our countries. The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly visible among us. The Forum being held in India is the largest-ever BRICS Business Forum.

Friends,

The theme of India’s BRICS Presidency is “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”

Over the past twelve years, India has made this mantra the foundation of its economic and trade policy. When it comes to resilience, India has made its supply chains more diversified and reliable, from energy to technology. It is this very resilience that has enabled India, even amid global uncertainties, to offer the world confidence in growth and stability.

We are rapidly expanding our roads, railways, ports, and airports. At the same time, we are building new capabilities in strategic sectors such as shipbuilding, semiconductors, quantum technology, critical minerals, and biotechnology. In these sectors, India is emerging as a hub of new opportunities for global businesses. Therefore, Make in India, Innovate with India, and Scale for the World.

Friends,

Today, India is witnessing a start-up revolution. With more than 200,000 start-ups and over 120 unicorns, India is emerging as a hub for global solutions. You will get a glimpse of this at the BRICS Bharat Innovates Expo.
