Our start-ups are transforming education and healthcare through AI, working on Green Hydrogen and Batteries, and breaking new frontiers in defence and space. Now, through BRICS as well, we must take these world-class innovations to global markets.

Friends,

Another distinctive feature of India’s innovation story is Innovation at Population Scale. India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has given new momentum to financial inclusion and digital transactions at population scale.

Today, 50% of the world’s real-time payments are powered by this technology. To build new solutions on this digital layer, we have provided industry and start-ups with an open ecosystem. We are proud that many countries are adopting India’s world-class ecosystem. Innovators from BRICS countries can also draw on this experience to develop new solutions for their own countries.

Friends,

Today, as trade barriers are increasing around the world, India is building economic bridges. Since 2014, we have entered into Free Trade Agreements with nearly 40 countries around the world. Our approach within BRICS is also the same, reduce barriers and expand opportunities for businesses.

Therefore, under our Presidency, we have established new cooperation networks in areas such as agriculture, healthcare, skills, and smart grids. To connect start-ups and SMEs with markets and finance, we have launched initiatives such as the BRICS Incubator Network, BRICS MSME Portal, and BRICS Startup Innovation Fund.

You can all benefit from these cooperation frameworks and further increase the exchange of investment and talent among our countries.

Friends,

Global trade can move forward only when sea lanes are secure, supply routes remain open, and seafarers are safe. That is why India is a staunch advocate of freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers.

The BRICS Women’s Business Alliance is also an important part of our vision. We want women entrepreneurs to lead our growth story. We are very pleased that nearly 200 women business leaders participated in the meeting of this Alliance held in India.

Friends,

As BRICS enters its third decade, I would urge the BRICS Business Council to consider … can you prepare a report on removing the top 10 trade barriers among BRICS countries? Can we support 100 BRICS startups every year to scale into other BRICS markets? Can we develop 1,000 new partnerships among our businesses? We should review our progress every year against these three benchmarks.

Let us transform BRICS’ ambition into action and our collective strength into global solutions. May BRICS move forward and help the world move forward as well.

Thank you all very much.
texts.pms-remarks-at-the-international-space-s:
My friend President Macron, Excellencies, Distinguished participants, Namaskar!

I am happy to be a part of the first International Space Summit. I thank President Macron for his gracious invitation and for taking this timely initiative. For centuries, space inspired our imagination. Today, it shapes life on Earth, from climate and crops to oceans and communities. The promise of space is infinite. Our responsibility is collective. As orbits become more crowded technologies more powerful, and actors more numerous our choices must be clear: cooperation over confrontation sustainability over short-term gain; and inclusion over exclusion.

Friends,

India’s approach is rooted in Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, that is One Earth, One Family, One Future. This spirit must now travel beyond Earth. We support a safe, secure, peaceful and sustainable space domain anchored in international law, dialogue and multilateral cooperation. Scientific data must serve the common good, with openness and integrity.

India’s space journey reflects this philosophy. ISRO, which stands at the heart of this journey, has earned global admiration for its excellence and cost-effective missions. Its capabilities serve farmers and fishermen, weather forecasting, disaster management and navigation. More than 430 satellites from 34 countries have travelled to space aboard Indian rockets. ISRO’s technologies and partnerships serve not only India, but the wider world.

Behind this global trust is the dedication and hard work of generations of Indian scientists, engineers and technicians. Working day and night, they have built ISRO’s global reputation mission by mission, success by success, and given India a place of pride among spacefaring nations.

Chandrayan-3 made India the first nation to land near the lunar south pole. Aditya-L1 is unlocking the secrets of the Sun. Last year, an Indian visited the International Space Station. Looking ahead, we aim to establish an Indian space station by 2035 and send an Indian to the Moon by 2040. In all these efforts, our guiding principle has been clear: their benefits must reach all humanity.

Alongside ISRO, India’s private space sector is also surging in a big way. The energy of enterprise is joining the excellence of ISRO. France has been a trusted partner since the Indian space program began at Thumba in the 1960s. Today, our cooperation spans Earth observation and advanced technologies, uniting scientific excellence with human purpose. We invite France and the world to be co-travellers in India’s next space frontier.

Friends,

Let the Space Summit in Paris send a clear message: we will explore together, innovate together and protect space together, for all humanity, and for generations to come. I convey my best wishes to all the participants.

Thank you.
texts.pms-address-during-inauguration-of-globa:
RBI Governor Shri Sanjay Malhotra ji, Global Fintech Fest Chairman Kris Gopalakrishnan ji, all innovators, leaders and investors of the fintech world, ladies and gentlemen.

I welcome all guests and delegates who have come from India and abroad to the Global Fintech Fest. I am happy that today another hat‑trick has been achieved. One hat‑trick was in 2024 when the government was formed for the third time, and another hat‑trick is my presence among you. This is my third consecutive year at the Global Fintech Fest. This hat‑trick shows how important you are for a developed India, how important your work is.

Friends,

Every time I come here, I see more youth, I feel more energy. I see the scope of possibilities expanding. It is clear that risk‑taking capacity is increasing, dreams are becoming bolder. And therefore, my confidence in the future of developed India is becoming stronger.

Friends,

Amidst this energy of fintech, Mumbai is also experiencing cultural energy at its peak these days. In just a few days, Ganeshotsav will begin in Maharashtra and across the country. In our tradition, Lord Ganesh is remembered before every auspicious work. Bowing to Ganapati Bappa, I extend my best wishes to all of you for Global Fintech Fest 2026.

Friends,

You all know well what the global situation is. The world is passing through a period of conflicts and uncertainty. Energy and commodity supply chains are under pressure, there are tensions in trade. These conditions have persisted for many months. The quarter from April to June was the most challenging. And even in such a situation, when India grows at 7.8 percent, the world gains new confidence. And this trust, I can clearly see on your faces here.

Friends,

Another example of this growing trust in India is our sovereign ratings. Recently, a Japanese credit rating agency upgraded India’s sovereign ratings to the A category. An upgrade is a matter of happiness, but very few people know that this fortune has come after three decades – after thirty years. This shows how assured the world is about India’s growth momentum, our macro‑economic stability, and the structural reforms carried out in recent years. And I repeat, India’s reform express will move forward at even greater speed.

Friends,

India’s fintech story has been extraordinary. And one of its biggest champions is our UPI. I spoke about it last year too. But this transformation is so big that whenever fintech is discussed, it will always be incomplete without UPI.

Friends,

Just a few days ago, on 25th August, UPI completed 10 years. Ten years ago, when I said that your bank would be at your fingertips, some people thought it impossible – and I am talking about well‑informed people, remember their faces. I am not talking about the millions of Indians whose bank accounts had just been newly opened then. Generations of theirs had never even seen the door of a bank. But today, ten years later, look – those same millions of people, who for generations were outside the banking system, have become the big drivers of fintech growth in India.

Friends,

Today, in the month of August alone, more than 2,400 crore transactions were done through UPI. That means, in just the time we have been sitting here, in 10 minutes alone, on average more than 5 million UPI transactions have taken place across the country. This is the impact because of which France’s President Macron said – he said that UPI is not just a tech story, it is a civilizational story.

And friends,

UPI is no longer limited to India. A few years ago, if someone had said that payments could be made abroad directly from an Indian bank account, hardly anyone would have believed it. But today, it is a reality. India’s UPI is now live in 11 countries. These are extraordinary figures, showing how long a journey we have traveled. But now the question is – should we be satisfied with this journey? Should we consider fintech’s success in India as final?

Friends,

I am completing 25 years in the ecosystem of policy and governance. And those who have seen me in these years know – Modi is not one to stop at a milestone, celebrate, and be satisfied. When one goal is achieved, I immediately begin preparing for an even bigger goal.

Friends,

Today our UPI has reached many countries. But this is only the first step. Our next goal should be to connect with the payment systems of those countries. We have already done this with Singapore. Because of this, transactions between India and Singapore happen just like between two neighborhoods of the same city. This same connection we must build with other countries, other markets. We must move forward with this goal. Wherever Indians live in large numbers, wherever India trades on a large scale, whichever country is ready to walk with us – we must work to connect them all.

Friends,

This is also necessary because abroad, a large number of Indians work. And Indians are the largest in the world in sending money back home. But today, a part of that money is lost in transaction costs. UPI can save Indians even in this, and money can reach Indian families more quickly.

Friends,

Today, how do you make payments in India with cards? This system runs on standards that were designed elsewhere. We adopted those standards and rules that others had created. At that time, we did not have our own option. But now we have our own option. Now we can create our own rules and standards, and connect them with the world. I have full confidence in all of you that you can do this.

Friends,

Technology is the most effective tool of inclusion. And UPI has demonstrated this. When it comes to fintech, its unique feature must be to reach where traditional models could not. Where traditional banks could not reach, where bank branches could not reach, UPI has taken the banking system to that place, to that person.

Friends,

Today, a large part of the fintech market is only payments. But now we must move to the next level, and move quickly. In the fintech market, along with payments, the share of credit transactions must increase, the share of insurance must increase, the share of savings, investments, and pensions must increase.

Friends,

I believe fintech can bring out that strength of the country which is still outside the reach of traditional financial models, or not being addressed properly. For a developed India, bringing out this strength is very necessary.

Friends,

We can already see the impact of this in the success of PM SVANidhi. Our street vendors are the backbone of cities. But they were outside the country’s banking system, outside the formal credit system. PM SVANidhi connected millions of street vendors to the formal system. And now these companions also have the SVANidhi credit card – that means they have a tool of formal credit access. And studies show that the average annual income of these beneficiaries has increased by more than 20 percent. Not only this, their families have seen improvements in housing, nutrition, healthcare access, and children’s education. That is why the government has decided to extend this scheme until 2030.

Friends,

PM SVANidhi would not have achieved this success if UPI did not exist. UPI has played a very big role in the success of this scheme. Learning from this experience, we must use the power of fintech to further increase economic activities. Let me give you an example from the world of capital and credit. There is a sister who runs a small shop. She receives digital payments every day. Now her income and expenses show a clear pattern. Her business is running well. She has moved beyond the level where small capital was enough. Now she needs goods, equipment to scale up her business, and for this she needs a little more money. This is not very large credit. And her business is still so small that traditional credit models cannot serve her efficiently. There are many such businesses whose needs fintech can analyze, anticipate, and address. And the number of such businesses is very large.

Friends,

Technology can help us study the economic activities of such businesses and design curated models for them. I believe the next chapter of fintech will be written here. We have shown speed and scale in payments. Now we must help increase the share of non‑payment transactions. For example, a delivery partner, or a person doing some small work – he earns every month, but he needs access to services like savings and pension products. Fintech can address the needs of such people. Similarly, fintech can make access easier to insurance products and other financial services. All these can be made just as simple, easy, and accessible as making a payment today with a QR code.

Friends,

The first quarter of the 21st century has ended. Now we are in the year 2026. The second quarter has brought even newer possibilities for us. Agentic AI, tokenization, quantum – such technologies are opening new doors of possibilities in the financial sector. Now the challenge before us is how to turn these possibilities into real impact. And for this, I want our fintech companies to set some tasks for themselves. And I want to place some suggestions before you. First – we must make cyber security in India top‑notch. Second – our industry must have its own ethical data protection standards. Third – we must build a strong fintech regulator‑industry innovation ecosystem. And fourth – we must have a fintech consumer protection index, on the basis of which every company can have a transparent rating. If we test ourselves on these parameters, India’s fintech sector can become the gateway of countless possibilities. We have the experience, and we have the way to implement it on the ground. Therefore, we must work quickly.

Friends,

The success story of Digital India is now ready for a new chapter. The success of our fintech story so far has been scale, scope, secure systems, democratization of technology, and public trust. Keeping these core values in mind, the fintech sector must focus on next‑generation innovation. With this appeal, once again I extend my best wishes to all of you. Thank you very much.
texts.pms-speech-during-the-namo-for-viksit-bh:
Bharat Mata ki Jai.

Bharat Mata ki Jai.

Governor of Gujarat Acharya Devvrat ji, the popular Chief Minister of Gujarat Shri Bhupendra Bhai Patel, many distinguished leaders from other states who have joined us online – Maharashtra Governor Jishnu Dev Varma ji, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis ji, Deputy CM Eknath Shinde ji, Deputy CM Sunetra Pawar ji, other ministers, MPs, MLAs, and the lakhs of citizens gathered there. On stage here, my colleagues from the Union Cabinet Ashwini Vaishnaw, Deputy CM and young leader Harsh Sanghvi, ministers of the Gujarat government, other public representatives present, and my dear brothers and sisters of Gujarat.

And especially, because this Maharaja Sayajirao University ground of Vadodara is hosting companions from different fields together, this festival of development is happening here all at once.

Friends,

Today I have come among you to give more speed to the journey of a developed India. Just a short while ago, projects worth thousands of crores of rupees connected to the country’s development were inaugurated and foundation stones laid here. I extend heartfelt congratulations to the people of the nation. On this festival of development, the way you all have carried out a cleanliness and welcome campaign across Vadodara city with a spirit of service, I heartily congratulate every citizen of Vadodara and appreciate them. And the color you have shown – yesterday I was watching a video, my chest swelled with pride. Wow! Is this my Vadodara? And now preparations for Ganeshotsav, later Navratri. During Ganeshotsav and Navratri, the whole of Gujarat’s attention is on Vadodara. And today I saw, for the past week, every family has created an atmosphere of cleanliness. I feel that this time when Lord Ganesh arrives, all blessings will shower upon Vadodara.

Friends,

This year from the Red Fort I called for the Saptdharas (Seven Streams) of resolve for a developed India. One of these streams is Gati Shakti. For a developed India we need connectivity that is smooth and also fast according to the times. Vadodara is the city of Gati Shakti University. Today, the last links of the Dedicated Freight Corridor have also been joined from here. Today, the project of more than 2,800 kilometers of Dedicated Freight Corridor has been completed. This is a very historic achievement for 21st‑century India.

Friends,

This Dedicated Freight Corridor is proof of how the work culture of the country has changed in the past 12 years. The idea of this corridor began in 2004. That means, I see all the youth here – when this idea began, many of you had not even been born. In 2006, a special company was created to carry out this work, and then until 2014, the files just kept moving from here to there. Files were traveling on tables, and unfortunately, even those files did not get a dedicated corridor. Files were stuck, hanging, wandering. And in 2014, the people of Vadodara, Gujarat, and the nation sent me from Gujarat to Delhi. The earlier government remained until 2014. You sent me, and they departed. The truth was that in seven–eight years – my young friends, listen carefully and remember – in seven–eight years not even one kilometer of the freight corridor was completed. If the country had continued at their pace, perhaps even after three–four generations it would not have been done. This was the condition they had left of a project meant to transform India’s logistics ecosystem.

Friends,

After 2014, the education and lessons you had given me here, what this land had taught me, the lessons I carried with me to Delhi – as soon as we reached there, we began to give speed to this project. Today, the 2,800‑kilometer corridor has been completed. And today the Eastern and Western Dedicated Freight Corridors are becoming the main foundation of the country’s trade and commerce.

Friends,

The Dedicated Freight Corridor is the lifeline of rapidly developing India. It has transformed India’s transportation sector. Earlier, passenger trains ran on the same tracks as freight trains. That meant both travel and transport were slow. But the Dedicated Freight Corridor has changed this situation. Today, on the Eastern and Western freight corridors, more than 430 freight trains run every day – 430 freight trains daily. Earlier, a freight train took six and a half hours to cover 100 kilometers. Now the same freight train covers 100 kilometers in less than half that time. Where sending goods by truck normally took 30 hours, on the Dedicated Freight Corridor the same distance is completed in 10–12 hours. That means, with freight trains running on this corridor, fuel is saved compared to trucks and trains, freight costs are reduced, time is saved, and the environment benefits. That means, investment was made on one track, and the benefits have been many.

Friends,

Through this freight corridor, the produce of farmers from eastern and western India is now reaching big markets more quickly. Many varieties of flowers, vegetables, fruits – items that spoil quickly depending on the season – now have a way to reach mandis and consumers at the right time. This has greatly benefited farmers.

Friends,

This freight corridor is remarkable for another reason. Recently, from JNPT Mumbai port to Vadodara, a double‑stack container freight train was operated. That means one container was placed on top of another, and the train ran. With this train, in one trip, goods equal to more than 250 trucks were transported from Mumbai to Vadodara – 250 trucks. Now, the “angry uncle” types will shout, “What will happen to the truck owners? Where will the trucks go? Those who bought trucks, what will happen to them?” So they have found new work. But in reality, now large quantities of goods can move quickly from one corner of the country to another.

Friends,

Along with the freight corridor, railways are now reaching places where they had not reached for decades. In Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra – the tribal areas here are also being connected to rail through this project. In earlier governments, in the budget, one or two trains would be announced, and they would beat drums about it for a whole year. Whereas today, throughout the year, one new train after another is being launched. Even in today’s program, several new trains have started. The new train will bring great convenience to the people of Vadodara, Chhota Udaipur, and Alirajpur.

Friends,

Roads, railways, metros, airports, gas pipelines, homes for the poor – when these things are built for crores of people in the country, life becomes easier, and at the same time, millions of employment opportunities are created for workers, from small to large. Take railways alone – this year’s rail budget has been more than 2.75 lakh crore rupees, which is many times higher compared to 12 years ago. That means the expenditure on railway modernization is creating thousands upon thousands of new jobs. And these jobs are created during construction itself. Once roads, railways, pipelines, ports, airports are built, then new industries start coming up around them, new businesses arrive, and these create new jobs.

Friends,

I have placed before the country the vision of Saptdharas (seven streams) of resolve for a developed India. One of these streams is manufacturing. And Vadodara city knows and understands this strength very well. How education, skill, and industry collaborate – Vadodara has reflected this for nearly 150 years. Decades ago, the journey here began with textiles and tiles manufacturing, which later advanced with oil and petrochemicals. In the past two–two and a half decades, Vadodara has become a major hub of MSMEs. And I remember, when I had just become Chief Minister, Vadodara always had a special claim on me. Every week some delegation would come, saying, “Do something for manufacturing in Vadodara.” Because when you came here, you would see Jyoti, LMB, GSFC – that was all, nothing else was visible. Today, how much has changed! Now this city is also known for the country’s first Made in India military transport aircraft. The C‑295 aircraft’s first flight has already been seen in the skies here. I heartily congratulate the people of Vadodara for attaining this pride.

Friends,

When we talk about the country’s manufacturing, I want to share another figure. In the past decade, India has become a major manufacturer of rail coaches, metro coaches, and rail engines. Since 2014, India has manufactured nearly 50,000 modern railway coaches. Listen to this figure – since 2014, India has made 50,000 modern coaches. The earlier government could not even build 50,000 toilets in 10 years. We have made 50,000 modern coaches, and nearly 250,000 wagons for freight trains have been added to Indian Railways.

Friends,

Now India is writing a new saga of manufacturing – from chip to ship. That means the parts are ours and the products are ours; a complete chain of self‑reliance will be built within India itself. We are seeing this in the case of solar power. For example, the floating solar plant project at Kadana Dam. A few years ago, setting up solar projects in the country was very expensive, because PV modules and all types of hardware had to be imported. But in recent years we have started manufacturing PV modules in India itself. Today we have developed a capacity of more than 200 gigawatts. And because of such self‑reliance, the PM Surya Ghar Free Electricity Scheme is expanding. So far, 5.5 million families in the country have installed solar plants on their rooftops. Among them, 1.1 million families are from Gujarat. So many families here have become electricity producers, and because of this, from production to installation and service, countless youths have got employment, and many new vendors have emerged.

Friends,

Those who spread the “echo of lies” can be found at every crossroads, but India’s youth walk with the roar of truth, move with the roar of truth, and live for the roar of truth. Our young companions are seeing how today the government is working with focus in every sector – solar, wind, hydro, nuclear.

Friends,

In the coming era, every modern sector will run on electricity, will depend on the electric ecosystem. For example, the chip industry, data centers, and industries connected to AI – their food and water is electricity. Therefore, if we want to become a superpower in AI before the world, the country must prepare and build its ecosystem. This is exactly what India is doing on the ground. That is why agreements are being made with some countries for uranium, with others for critical minerals and rare earth minerals. All this effort is being made day and night to secure the future of the country’s youth – for your future.

Friends,

The world is changing rapidly, so the needs of the world are also changing. And in the same way, our methods of study and learning are also changing. Earlier the focus was only on degrees, but now along with degrees, the focus is also on skills. The importance of skill is increasing. It has become a major need that youth should have skills, and those skills should be upgraded from time to time. That is why today we are reshaping our education policy, our teaching and training institutions in a new form. And with this spirit, from the Red Fort I also made two major announcements for youth power. The first announcement is connected with the country’s traditional need. You all know that in our country millions of youth prepare for competitive exams. Every year, a large part of the income of our middle‑class families is spent on coaching for these children. Our effort is to save the money of such poor and middle‑class families. That is why now the government is moving forward to provide students with free online coaching arrangements. And coaching will be given by India’s best teachers. For our youth who are preparing, the government itself will take care of their coaching.

Friends,

It is equally important for India’s youth to be proficient in AI. We want our young generation to be prepared for AI. It is not that the need for AI learners is only in the IT sector. If someone knows this skill, he can create new AI solutions for agriculture. He can develop technology in the field of healthcare. He can increase productivity in manufacturing. He can start his own startup in robotics. Therefore, it is necessary that we have youth who understand AI and use AI for the industries of the country and the world. The government is going to launch a major campaign for this.

Friends,

This period of India is unprecedented. This is the era of the rise of India’s youth power. This time will not return again in India’s life. Therefore, we must keep the goal of a developed India in 2047 as supreme. We must make India developed. With this call, once again I extend many congratulations to you all for the development works.

Now I have one task for the people of Vadodara – will you do it? Surely? You have made Vadodara so clean, it took so much effort. I saw our youth working day and night in cleaning. But let us decide once that now we will not allow Vadodara to become dirty again. If each of us takes the pledge, “I will not create dirt myself,” then will Vadodara become dirty? Will Vadodara become dirty? Then Diwali will shine brilliantly, Navratri will be celebrated splendidly, Ganeshotsav will be adorned with glory. So this much work will surely be done.

Well done.

Thank you.

texts.pms-remarks-during-inauguration-of-swami:
Respected Mahant Swami, honored representatives of the French government, distinguished guests, members of the Indian community, all Hari devotees connected from across the world, ladies and gentlemen – Jai Swaminarayan!

Today, in the capital of France, Paris, the grand Swaminarayan temple is being inaugurated. This inauguration is a new milestone in the cultural relations between India and France. With the blessings of revered saints and the noble custodians of the Sanatan tradition, today this inauguration platform has become a stage of the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam – “the world is one family.” By the grace of Lord Swaminarayan and the affection and blessings of our saints, it is my fortune that I always get the opportunity to be connected with such sacred occasions. Even today, though I am not physically present among you in Paris, in mind and heart I feel myself to be right there with you.

Friends,

On this occasion, I also respectfully remember Param Pujya Pramukh Swami Maharaj. In ancient times, India’s cultural and spiritual glory was immense, and he began a campaign for its renaissance. Today its light is spreading across Europe and the entire world. In 2024, the grand temple in Abu Dhabi was inaugurated. Today thousands of people go there for darshan. And now here in Paris, the construction of the Swaminarayan temple – this continuity of creation – is proof of the resolve and strength of our saints. I express gratitude to Pujya Mahant Swami for this sacred work, I bow at his feet. I extend heartfelt congratulations to the BAPS Swaminarayan organization and to millions of Hari devotees on this occasion.

Friends,

Through BAPS, when temples are consecrated in different countries, India’s ancient ideas and human values also travel with them. And India’s thought says: “Samanam manah saha chittamesham” – may our minds be united, may our hearts be connected. Therefore, today when such a grand temple has been built in France, it will enrich France’s diversity, and it will also energize the cultural relations between India and France.

Friends,

In recent years, India and France’s relations have reached new heights. Together with my friend President Macron, both countries are building a Special Global Strategic Partnership. From technology, AI, and defense to space and climate action, we are moving forward with new speed and new energy. We are also celebrating 2026 as the India–France Year of Innovation. This strategic partnership is special because it rests on the strong foundation of our old cultural and political ties. History is witness – the sacrifices of Indian soldiers in France are still alive in the temple of memory. Those interested in languages also know how French scholars played a crucial role in popularizing Sanskrit. The writings of Romain Rolland on Ramakrishna Paramhansa and Swami Vivekananda brought our societies closer. From Paris to the Puducherry Aurobindo Ashram, “The Mother’s” spiritual journey inspired countless Indian and French seekers.

Friends,

Decades ago, Srila Prabhupada Swami also came to France. Through ISKCON he began a new chapter of spiritual relations between India and France. Today yoga too has become a medium of people‑to‑people connection between India and France. The pictures from in front of the Eiffel Tower on International Yoga Day are examples of yoga’s popularity in France. And now, through this grand BAPS temple, a new chapter is being added to our cultural relations.

Friends,

These days, there are discussions about India–France joint ventures. The Swaminarayan temple has added a new dimension to this possibility. This temple is “Made in India” and “Built in France.” Many of its stones were carved in India. India’s ancient craftsmanship has joined here with modern engineering in France. In Paris, this grand temple has taken shape. Therefore, I hope this temple will stand for centuries as a symbol of cooperation and possibilities between India and France.

Friends,

Swaminarayan temples have always been not only centers of devotion but also of service. I have been told that this temple too will become such a center of service projects. I am confident that the voices of Indian culture that will arise from here will benefit people across Europe. In the future, whenever I get the time, I will surely make the effort to come and have darshan in this temple. With these words, once again I extend many congratulations on this auspicious occasion to all the guests present, all families, all Hari devotees, and the entire Indian diaspora.

Thank you very much!

Merci beaucoup!

Jai Swaminarayan!
texts.pms-address-during-the-centenary-celebra:
My colleagues in the Union Cabinet Shri Prahlad Joshi ji, DU Vice Chancellor Yogesh Singh ji, SRCC Principal Simrit Kaur ji, Ajay ji, Mallika ji, Rajat ji, all companions connected with SRCC, faculty, staff, SRCC alumni, and my young friends!

I am the sixth player. Today’s occasion is very historic for Shri Ram College of Commerce, and equally important for the country’s education world. Here, many generations who have been part of SRCC have gathered together. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to all of you for this centenary celebration of SRCC. I respectfully pay tribute to its founder, Sir Shri Ram ji, and bow to his vision.

Friends,

When a person lives for 100 years, he is considered an ocean of experiences. And when an institution completes 100 years, it becomes an ocean of achievements and inspirations. In its 100‑year journey, SRCC has shaped generations, connecting them to a bright future. Those who came studied, and those who left went out as well‑shaped individuals. The journey of this college began in Daryaganj, in a small place, and today that small college has become a huge tree. A tree that has given shade to many generations, and enriched them with its coolness. Even today, in DU, when someone asks which college, saying SRCC itself is a flex in itself.

Friends,

The alumni of SRCC have also been very special. If I say in your language, the alumni here are the OGs, who carried SRCC’s name across the world, making their mark in different fields. Rajat ji mentioned a long list. And I too have had the opportunity to work with some of them. Our Arun Jaitley ji studied here. And I can say that perhaps there was never a meeting with him where he did not narrate some incident of SRCC. Sometimes I would get tired, because he would repeat the same incident again and again. In my team today, brother Sanjeev Sanyal also studied here. Many other companions are here too. And it is not that only people from the world of economics came out of here – many artists, leaders, lawyers, judges have also come from here. That is, SRCC people have created a stir in every field. They may not all be giants, but they certainly created a stir.

Friends,

For the past few days, this program has been much discussed. Especially people are remembering my 2013 address. People have listened to it again, read it again. It is possible that the new generation has also revisited it. That speech, I can say, became a wave, a movement. And even today, 13–14 years later, the impact of that gathering, that address, remains.

Friends,

Then, in your place, your seniors were sitting. And I was then a Chief Minister, but also a member of the country’s main opposition party. And perhaps people then expected that I would make long attacks on the central government of that time, shower accusations.

But friends,

Even while being in opposition, even while being a critic of the then government, I did not use that platform for that. I placed a vision, spoke positive things. Whatever I said then was my conviction. I have always lived those words, those dreams. I have always walked that path – dedicating myself wholeheartedly for the country, living with the spirit of serving the nation. That inner world of mine, that emotional universe, on that day in 2013, from this very platform, came out one by one in a garland of words. And I spoke at length. Then I asked the students if I should continue, and they loudly said, “Yes, continue.”

Friends,

That day I gave the example of a glass of water, and it was much discussed in the country. I explained the three perspectives of looking at a glass half‑filled with water. One, those who see the glass as half full of water. Second, those who see the glass as half empty. And third, those who see the glass as completely full – half with water and half with air.

Friends,

This was the time when the country was sunk in the swamp of despair. Even then I said that I do not see the glass as half, I do not see it as incomplete – I see the glass as completely full. Half with water, half with air. And at that time you all must have been in school, but today if you go on the internet and read the news of 2013 and around that period, you will realize what the situation was. And I urge the youth – just look once at that period of 2013 on the internet, the headlines around my speech then. Whether newspapers or TV channels, what were the headlines then? Let me give you a glimpse of those headlines. Now there is a gang that will cut my words into small pieces and put them in my account, so I warn beforehand that what I am telling you is what dominated the media in 2013, such as:

• Indian soldiers killed on the LoC – today’s generation may find it strange that such things happened, but they did.

• World Bank lowered GDP growth forecast.

• Current account deficit at an all‑time high.

• Inflation rate around ten percent.

• Industrial sector caught in recession.

• Helicopter deal bribery exposed.

• Bomb blasts in Hyderabad.

These were the headlines of that time. I am sure today’s students do not know all this. These things show what the condition of the country was then. Growth was on the floor and inflation was on the ceiling. Scams were at their peak and the corrupt roamed fearlessly. The economy was in bad shape, everywhere there was talk of policy paralysis. The world counted India among the “Fragile Five.” Terrorists were unchecked and Pakistan was uncontrollable. That is, then there was nothing but despair and frustration.

Friends,

That was the day when on every front the country was struggling, and this is today – today those spreading terrorism are subdued. If Pakistan does any nefarious act, India’s forces enter their home and strike. From Jammu & Kashmir to the North East, peace has increased. Maoist terror, Naxalism has been broken. The world that was then worried about policy paralysis in India, today talks about India’s policy dynamism. Then the world called India part of the Fragile Five, today the world sees India becoming the fastest‑growing major economy. Just in the past week, many positive news items have come about India’s economy. The 7.8 percent quarterly growth has boosted the nation’s enthusiasm, and in the same period a Japanese credit rating agency has upgraded India’s rating.

And friends,

This 7.8 percent growth has come at a time when war is going on in West Asia, when there have been many trade‑related obstacles. To achieve such growth at such a time shows India’s capability in itself.

Friends,

I know, you also know, those who were infamous for pushing India into the Fragile Five, they cannot digest these figures. But you all understand the numbers seriously. Between April and June, electricity production increased by 9 percent, vehicle sales grew by more than 20 percent. In that too, two‑wheelers grew by 20 percent, and three‑wheelers by nearly 30 percent. That means consumer demand is running, and commercial activity is strong. Growth in steel and cement consumption increased by 8 percent. That means construction, housing, infrastructure, and industrial activity are all rising. That means India is growing, and creating new employment opportunities too. Despite this, for those who saw the glass half empty in 2013, their thinking remains the same even today. For them the glass will always be half empty. When I speak of the glass, I am not speaking of anything being empty.

Friends,

In 2013, speaking here at SRCC, I also spoke of P2G2 – Pro‑People Good Governance. Those who ran governments for long had a style – wake up only when there is fire, dig a well only when there is drought. I spoke of changing this approach. And after forming government in 2014, we have shown this in action. Let me give you an example.

Friends,

Recently, the Jan Dhan Yojana completed 12 years. Today you are living in a completely different era of fintech, but those were also the days of 2013 when students from villages or small towns had to struggle a lot even to open savings bank accounts. At that time our population had crossed 1.25 billion, but by March 2014, more than 50 percent of the country’s population did not even have bank accounts. And those outside the banking system were mostly the poor, women, migrant laborers, students. That is why we brought the Jan Dhan scheme, and in the past 12 years, because of Jan Dhan Yojana, nearly 600 million new bank accounts have been opened. Today almost every family in the country is connected to the banking system. This became the foundation of India’s fintech revolution.

Friends,

Now think also about those people who opposed even connecting millions of people to the banking system. In fact, such people enjoyed only when the glass was half full, so that the poor ordinary citizens kept circling around them. This “mai‑baap” culture they had continued for decades. But this is Modi – standing like a rock before those who liked the mai‑baap culture.

Friends,

There is an old saying: truth fears no fire. I have courage, and that is why I am reminding you of what I said that day, bringing my report card before you. I know that before the roar of truth, the echo of lies cannot stand.

Friends,

In that 2013 program itself, when I said that we must work on Made in India, the people of the old ecosystem of that time could not even understand it. They thought that in that era of despair, Made in India would not be possible at all! And those who grew up in that thinking still mock Made in India.

But friends,

Today you are seeing the brand value of Make in India. Let me explain with an example. Today every hand has a smartphone. The world’s biggest phone brands are making India their base. Made in India smartphones are reaching every corner of the world. In 2014, India imported most of its mobile phones. Today India exports mobile phones worth more than 2.5 lakh crore rupees.

Friends,

I am not a person who takes small and easy targets. I set big goals for the country, and I put my whole life into achieving them. Look at the defense sector. Earlier, most things for India’s armed forces were bought from abroad. As soon as I came, I told the defense people – make a negative list. First they made a list of 500 items, saying these we will not bring from outside. Then they made 1,000, then 3,000. Army, Navy, Air Force – many times even for a small piece of equipment they had to wait for months. We made a plan together with the armed forces, made lists of items, then told Indian companies to make all these. And today you see, the country’s defense manufacturing is at its all‑time high. Today India is producing defense equipment worth nearly 2 lakh crore rupees. In 2013–14, we exported defense equipment worth 600–700 crore rupees. Today this figure has reached nearly 40,000 crore rupees. And these achievements are possible because today a vibrant defense manufacturing ecosystem is being built in the country.

Friends,

I have trust in the country, trust in the country’s capability, trust in you youth. And on the basis of this trust I speak of a developed India. I am confident that we 1.4 billion Indians together will make our country developed and self‑reliant.

• In the coming time, India will be a hub of manufacturing.

• In the coming time, Hindustan will be a hub of research and innovation.

• India will be a superpower of agricultural exports.

My young friends,

• India will have its own space station.

And you will also see the day when India will host an Olympics in such a way that the world will be left watching in awe.

And these are not just words, these are our resolutions. And to turn these resolutions into reality, continuous work is happening in the country.

Friends,

Right now your life is running in SRCC mode. Whether it is tea at the co‑op, discussions over cold coffee, last‑minute notes for exams, rushing for printouts, or the hard work put into Crossroads and the Business Conclave – you have made every moment here a memory of your life. But outside this campus, a new world awaits you. You will meet two kinds of people. One, those who positively transform the power of society into the power of the nation. The second species are those who, whenever any work begins, become the “angry uncle.” Their favorite job is to oppose everything. Their permanent dialogue is: “What is the need for this? What is the need for this?” That is the permanent line of every such uncle. When we were building the world’s tallest statue, these uncles tightened their belts and said, “What is the need for this?” When we started work on the high‑speed train, they again said, “What is the need for this?” When we brought UPI, these same people said, “Why UPI? What is the need for UPI?” When we spoke of making chips, again they said, “What is the need for this?” When we built the new Parliament building, they said, “What is the need for this?” When we built a memorial for our brave military commanders who gave the supreme sacrifice for the nation, again they came out saying, “What was the need for this?” But India has answered all such uncles – whatever is necessary for the country, no one can stop India from doing it.

Friends,

Today India is moving forward with a different temperament. Work that earlier took decades is now happening within just a few years. Let me give you another example with full facts. India’s first electric train ran in 1925. Your college started in 1926, but the train ran in 1925. After that, until 2014 – that is, 90 years – less than 30 percent of railway lines were electrified. In just 12 years, we have shown nearly 100 percent electrification of railway lines.

Friends,

This speed in India’s policy decisions is being seen and understood by the rest of the world. That is why they are increasing their partnerships with India. In the past decade, trade agreements and free trade agreements have been signed with nearly 40 countries. Because of this, new markets are opening for leather, textiles, fruits and vegetables, our processed food, shrimp, and many other products. Who better than you knows what it means when new markets open, when tariffs are reduced for India’s goods and services. This is creating a new sky of opportunities for India’s youth.

Friends,

Today, compared to 2013, the country is far more secure economically and socially. But seeing this, some people’s restlessness and frustration are increasing. You must have heard my speech on 15th August. For such people, I gave a dose of homeopathy from the Red Fort – a small homeopathy pill. And you know, they say the nature of homeopathy is that when you start the medicine, at first the illness flares up even more. That is the nature of homeopathy. So from the Red Fort I gave a homeopathy pill – “mental Naxal.” This mental Naxal treatment, as I said, first flares up the illness for some time, and then begins the cure. In the same way, as soon as I gave the mental Naxal pill, all the mental Naxals started coming out. And those who are promoting this illness, now the public is seeing their true colors too.

Friends,

I have said so many things, some people may think – oh, what is the big deal, it was a country of 1.4 billion, it was easy, what new did Modi do? But was it really so easy? Let me take you back once again to the old days. Remember when you were in school. In 2013, when the disaster struck Kedarnath, the entire government was shaken. They did not know what to do, how to do it. In 2008, when the banking crisis came, the government of that time tried to hide behind that crisis until 2014, not daring to even touch it. India’s entire banking system was brought to the brink of collapse. In 2008 itself, when the horrific terrorist attack happened in Mumbai, the government then came under external pressure, but did not even show the courage to teach Pakistan a lesson.

Friends,

In the past 12 years, many disasters have struck the country, we have faced huge cyclones, but the nation has faced them strongly. In the past 6 years, very big crises have come. First the pandemic of corona, which shut down the whole world. Then the war broke out between Russia and Ukraine. After that, the era began of weaponizing trade and supply chains. Then came the crisis in West Asia. Every time it was said, now India will not survive. And those who are my “special admirers” were happy thinking – now Modi is trapped, now Modi will fall, now he will be crushed. But the blessings of my country’s people have such strength, such strength, that every wish of those who wanted India’s downfall has been left unfulfilled.

Friends,

Now in the 21st century, a world of new opportunities is before us. I am happy that you are ambitious, because ambition cannot be taught from a textbook. Ambition comes from the environment that inspires you to dream big. Today our young companions say – if I do something, I will start a startup, if I build a company, I will make it a unicorn. I will join sectors like space and drones, I will do something big. I will build cutting‑edge AI solutions, I will innovate in agriculture. Thirteen years ago, your seniors could not even dream such dreams. But today you are dreaming them, because in today’s India an ecosystem has been built to support those dreams.

Friends,

Now is the time to set big goals and achieve them. Just recently from the Red Fort I said some things. I want to repeat them among you. Take a pledge – why can’t India have global consulting firms? Why can’t our accounting firms, our legal firms, our financial firms become global leaders? We proudly say that today Indians are leading the world’s top companies. If Indians are leading the world’s top companies, then why can’t companies created by Indians lead the world?

Friends,

All this is possible. For this you have both networks and knowledge.

Friends,

Our inspiration, your inspiration, is also the SRCC college crest. It has two beautiful symbols. One is the rising sun, and the other is the ship moving forward in the sea. The sun, which shows direction, and the ship, which moves forward in that direction. We must walk on such new paths, where the sun is ours, the sea is ours. The boat is ours, the sailor is ours. The courage to write victory on the waves is ours. The flight is ours, the sky is ours. The spirit to face strong winds is ours. The dream is ours, the resolve is ours, the banner of self‑reliant India is ours. On the path of developed India, every step rising swiftly is ours. Once again, on this special occasion, I extend my many best wishes to all connected with SRCC.

Vande Mataram.
texts.pms-press-statement-during-the-joint-pre:
Your Excellency, Prime Minister, Delegates from both countries, Friends from media, Namaskar!

I am delighted to warmly welcome the Prime Minister on his first visit to India.

This is certainly his first visit to India, but he has a long-standing association with India. He served as the Mayor of Antwerp for many years and has always supported the large Indian community in Antwerp and India–Belgium diamond trade.

Friends,

The roots of India–Belgium relations run deep in history. The courage and sacrifice of thousands of Indian soldiers in Belgium during the First World War are an important part of our shared memory.

Today, democratic values, market economy, and deep people-to-people ties make us natural partners.

Friends,

Ten years ago, I had the opportunity to visit Belgium, and I am very pleased that our partnership has made remarkable progress over the past decade.

Today, the scope of our cooperation has expanded beyond traditional sectors to strategic areas such as defence and clean energy. We are working together on advanced defence equipment, such as the Zorawar tank. In Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh, we are developing one of the world’s largest green ammonia projects.

Friends,

Today, the world is going through a period of great upheaval. Conflicts continue to persist in many parts of the world. Whether it is food, fuel, or supply chains, every sector is being impacted by uncertainty.

In this challenging environment, India’s economy has maintained its momentum. We recorded 7.8% growth in the last quarter. Today, India’s growth story is becoming a source of confidence and new opportunities for the world.

Friends,

At the beginning of this year, we concluded the historic India–European Union Free Trade Agreement. This unprecedented cooperation between two of the world’s largest democratic powers will also give new impetus to global stability, development, and shared prosperity.

India’s sustained economic progress and this Agreement have opened new avenues for our economic relations. Today, we have taken several important steps to translate these possibilities into concrete outcomes.

Friends,

For Belgian companies, we have established an Investment Fast-Track Mechanism in India. We have decided to make the India–Belgium Business Forum a regular mechanism. We will strengthen coordination among the financial, fintech, and regulatory institutions of both countries.

Through all these initiatives, we will realise our goal of doubling bilateral trade over the next five years.

Friends,

Defence and security cooperation is a key pillar of our relationship. Today, we agreed to enhance military exchanges and training cooperation between the two countries.

The agreements between our governments and defence industries will open up new opportunities for defence co-development and co-production. We will also further strengthen intelligence sharing and cooperation between our agencies in combating crime.

Friends,

A clean energy future and reliable supply chains are our shared priorities. The MOU on Renewable Energy signed today will give new momentum to our sustainability cooperation. In critical minerals, we have decided to enhance cooperation in processing and recycling.

Belgium’s expertise in semiconductors and India’s scale are complementary to each other. In this direction, we will work together to connect Belgium’s IMEC Institute with India’s semiconductor ecosystem.

Friends,

People-to-people ties are the greatest strength of our relationship. Today, we agreed to strengthen connections between our start-ups and enhance capacity building in the maritime sector.

We will also strengthen university and research cooperation. And, to facilitate talent mobility, we will soon conclude a “Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement”.

Friends,

Today, we also had detailed discussions on regional and global developments. Both India and Belgium believe in the rule of law, dialogue, and diplomacy.

Whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, we support all efforts aimed at an early end to conflicts and the restoration of peace. And eliminating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations is our shared commitment.

Your Excellency,

Last month, Belgium and the Netherlands jointly hosted the Hockey World Cup. I congratulate you on the successful organisation of this grand World Cup. I also commend our players for their hard work and performance.

Diamonds have long been a link between India and Belgium. Today, we are transforming this historic connection into a new and more comprehensive relationship.

I am confident that today’s discussions mark the beginning of a new chapter in our bilateral relations. Once again, I extend a warm welcome to you and your delegation to India.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-statement-at-the-26th-sco-summit:
President of Kyrgyzstan,

Excellencies,

Namaskar!

It is a matter of great pleasure for me to be here amongst all of you on this special occasion of the 25th anniversary of the SCO.

I sincerely thank President Japarov for the warm welcome and gracious hospitality extended to us in Bishkek.

We had the privilege of being here yesterday, on the occasion of Kyrgyzstan’s Independence Day. I once again extend my warmest congratulations to the President and the people of Kyrgyzstan.

And today, on the occasion of Uzbekistan’s Independence Day, I extend my warmest congratulations to the President and the people of Uzbekistan as well.

During the spectacular Opening Ceremony of the World Nomad Games, we all caught a glimpse of Kyrgyzstan’s rich culture and our shared heritage. This shared heritage and our deep people-to-people connections are among the great strengths of the SCO family.

Friends,

Over the past twenty-five years, the SCO has developed a strong tradition of dialogue and cooperation across the vast expanse of Eurasia. Together, we have made valuable contributions not only to the well-being of our people, but also to the advancement of humanity. Over these twenty-five years, we have laid a strong foundation for cooperation. In the next twenty-five years, our goal should be to translate this cooperation into tangible outcomes.

At a time when the world is passing through uncertainty and instability, we must transform our shared geography into shared opportunities. And through our efforts, we must bring about positive change in the lives of our people.

Friends,

At the previous meeting, I had outlined the three main pillars of India’s vision for the SCO:

S – Security,

C – Connectivity, and

O – Opportunity

The time has come to move these three pillars beyond vision and translate them into concrete outcomes. The first and foremost requirement for this is peace and security. Terrorism continues to pose a serious challenge to humanity as a whole. In the fight against terrorism, we cannot remain confined to an action-reaction approach.

We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorist financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens. We must speak with one voice and make it clear that there can be no place for double standards on this serious issue.

We must send a strong message to countries that use terrorism as an instrument of policy and provide safe haven and support to terrorists that terrorism can never be a strategic asset for anyone.

Our shared aspiration for a peaceful and secure Eurasia is also closely linked to peace and stability in Afghanistan. India has been contributing to the development and provision of humanitarian assistance to the people of Afghanistan and will continue to do so.

In today’s interconnected world, the scope of security has become even broader. The crisis in West Asia has demonstrated that a conflict in one region does not remain confined to that region. Its impact is felt across the world, affecting energy security, maritime trade, and supply chains. The countries of the Global South bear the greatest brunt of such disruptions. Therefore, India has consistently called for all tensions and conflicts to be resolved not on the battlefield, but through dialogue and diplomacy.

Drug trafficking is not merely a crime; it is a serious threat to our younger generation and regional security. The Centres being established under the SCO to address challenges such as security threats, organised crime, information security, and narcotics are a positive step. We must make these Centres an effective instrument for practical coordination and timely action.

Friends,

The second pillar of our shared development is strong and reliable connectivity. India supports all efforts that connect markets, facilitate trade, and open up new avenues for development. However, it is equally essential that such efforts respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries. This is also the fundamental spirit of the SCO Charter.

Going forward, the scope of connectivity will become even broader. Along with roads, railways, and air corridors, we must simplify customs processes, promote digital documentation, and make logistics networks more efficient.

Friends,

The third pillar is — Opportunity.

It means that the benefits of SCO cooperation should reach our people directly. Our greatest strength is the connections between our people. For India, the SCO is a confluence of great civilisations, cultures, and ideas. Over the next twenty-five years of the SCO, people-to-people ties should remain at the heart of our cooperation.

The true measure of our success should be how many new opportunities our efforts create for young people, how many new markets open up for our entrepreneurs, how much our farmers benefit from technology, and how much better the lives of our citizens become.

This is the true meaning of “Security, Connectivity, and Opportunity.”

Our cooperation in the SCO should not be merely government-driven; it should also be people-driven. I am pleased that, under Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship, special emphasis has been placed on youth engagement within the SCO. India has taken initiatives such as the SCO Start-up Forum, Young Authors’ Conclave, and Young Scientists’ Forum.

Last year, India proposed the SCO Civilizational Dialogue Forum. I am pleased that its first session will be held in India this year. I am confident that with the active participation of all of you, this forum will become a strong platform for vibrant dialogue within the SCO.

Friends,

Kyrgyzstan’s great literary figure, Chingiz Aitmatov, gave the world a beautiful and profound thought. He said that we often focus more on the things that divide us, and less on the things that unite us.

This message is equally relevant for the SCO today. Our diversity is our identity, and our shared purpose is our strength. From Bishkek, we should move forward with this resolve:

From shared geography to shared opportunities,

from vision to outcomes,

and from government-driven cooperation to people-driven partnership.

With the same belief and commitment, India is ready to contribute to the SCO family’s shared journey.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-press-statement-during-the-joint-pre:
Your Excellency, My Friend, Mister President, Delegates from both countries, Friends from the media, Namaskar !

I sincerely thank the President and the people of Uzbekistan for the warm and affectionate welcome extended to me and my delegation in Tashkent.

This is my fourth visit to Uzbekistan. It reflects the closeness of our relations, our close coordination, and our deep friendship.

For nearly a decade, I have had the privilege of working with the President. During this period, I have had the opportunity to meet him more than ten times.

His positive and forward-looking approach, along with his spirit of continuous learning, is truly inspiring. I sincerely commend him for his deep friendship towards India and his unwavering commitment to our relationship.

Friends,

Uzbekistan is at the heart of Central Asia, and at the heart of India’s engagement with the region. India and Uzbekistan share a deep convergence of perspectives and aspirations. At the heart of both “Yangi Uzbekistan” and “Viksit Bharat 2047” are our youth, innovation, inclusive growth, and modern technology. Guided by this shared vision, we are working for the well-being and prosperity of the people of both countries.

This year marks the 15th anniversary of our Strategic Partnership. On this special occasion, we have decided to elevate our relationship to the level of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

Today, we have charted an ambitious agenda to take our partnership forward in this new framework with greater momentum and concrete outcomes.

Our bilateral trade has crossed one billion dollars. We have now set a target of five billion dollars in bilateral trade by 2030. To achieve this, we will systematically address issues related to market access, connectivity, banking, and payment systems.

We will work together to enhance win-win cooperation in infrastructure development. Cooperation in Digital Public Infrastructure, Artificial Intelligence, critical minerals, clean energy, space, and nuclear energy is making our relationship future-ready.

Friends,

Our strengths in agriculture and healthcare are complementary to each other. By combining Uzbekistan’s expertise in horticulture with India’s modern agricultural practices, we will contribute to the food security of both countries.

Uzbekistan’s medicinal herbs and India’s expertise in Ayurveda are also a natural combination. The agreement reached today on Traditional Medicine will give further impetus to our joint efforts in this area.

Our endeavour is to ensure that our partnership is not confined to our two capitals. Therefore, we are working towards establishing partnerships between our cities and states. These partnerships will help foster sustained direct linkages in areas such as urban management, industry, education, tourism, and culture.

The close defence and security cooperation between our two countries reflects the deep mutual trust that underpins our relationship. Going forward, we will promote direct linkages, co-production, and co-development between the defence industries of our two countries.

We believe that terrorism, extremism, and separatism pose serious challenges to the entire region.

Our shared resolve to adopt a policy of zero tolerance towards them has been, and will continue to be, unwavering.

Friends,

The deepest roots of our relationship lie in our shared heritage. Today, we placed special emphasis on further strengthening these bonds.

We will work together for the preservation of Uzbekistan’s Buddhist heritage sites. Promoting exchanges between the youth of our two countries, particularly students and professionals, is a high priority for us. Today, we agreed on a Programme of Cooperation to promote tourism between the two countries. I am pleased that today we are going to announce scholarships to promote the Hindi language in Uzbekistan.

Sports is also emerging as an important dimension of our cooperation. Last year, the 20-year-old Uzbek Grandmaster Sindarov won the FIDE World Cup in Goa. He is now set to face India’s 20-year-old chess champion, Gukesh, in November. When these two young stars meet across the chessboard, the entire world will be watching this exciting contest. I also extend my very best wishes for the Chess Olympiad to be held in Samarkand next month. In the times ahead, traditional sports such as Kurash and Kabaddi will also bring renewed energy to our sporting partnership.

Today’s discussions have charted a clear course for the future of our relations. A stronger India-Uzbekistan partnership will be a powerful force for peace, progress and prosperity in Central Asia.

Excellency,

Once again, I thank you very much for your friendship and for the fruitful discussions we had today.

In two days, Uzbekistan will celebrate the 35th anniversary of its Independence. On behalf of the 1.4 billion people of India, I extend my warmest congratulations and best wishes to you and all the citizens of Uzbekistan on this occasion.

Thank you very much.
texts.pms-address-in-the-137th-episode-of-mann:
My dear countrymen, Namaskar!

I welcome you all once again to this new episode of ‘Mann Ki Baat’. All of you know that this is a platform where we bring to the fore new initiatives and discuss the innovative ideas of our fellow countrymen. Many of these ideas are the result of people investing their boundless energy into them.

Friends,

Some time ago, someone wrote on social media, “On the auspicious occasion of Ashadhi Ekadashi, I am delighted to announce the launch of my initiative to make history interesting.” They further explained that the idea is quite simple: visit the website and select any year. There you can easily find out which ruler ruled over what part of India at that time. I found this quite interesting too and thought of learning more about it. I discovered that this work has been done by Shriman Krishna Seshadri, a resident of Mumbai. Interestingly, Krishna ji has kept the website’s name very simple: www.bharatrajya.com. The effort he has put in should reach all of you; that is why I thought, why not speak directly to Shri Krishna ji!

Friends,

Krishna ji is joining us on the phone.

Prime Minister: Namaste, Krishna ji.

Krishna Seshadri: Namaste, Sir, Namaste.

Prime Minister: My friend, I’ve learned that you neither belong to the tech world nor are you a history teacher; yet, you utilized technology to create a website dedicated to history. I am very curious—how did this all come about?

Krishna Seshadri: Thank you, Sir; it is a great privilege to speak with you. To tell you a little about myself: I was an engineer, then I pursued an MBA and entered the field of marketing. However, throughout all this, I maintained a deep interest in history – something I’ve had since childhood. So, I always wanted to do something on history – how to make it interesting and I felt there was immense scope for improvement and change in how we teach history… we could present history to reach people as a story.

Prime Minister: Krishna-ji, what aspect of Indian history did you feel needed to be known by the maximum number of people?

Krishna Seshadri: Sir, the way Indian history is taught in our schools and colleges often focuses on the perspective of a single empire or kingdom, with those specific empires receiving disproportionate attention. Consequently, we remain unaware of many other great empires—such as the Cholas, the Pallavas, the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir, or the Ahoms, who preserved their culture and value system in Assam for at least 600 years. So, I decided to create a site that introduces people to these great empires.

Prime Minister: Krishna-ji, you work so hard; let me ask you a hypothetical question. If you had the opportunity to converse with any three figures from Indian history, who would you choose, and why?

Krishna Seshadri: Yes, Sir. First, I would speak to Rajaraja Chola or Rajendra Chola – who was one of the most powerful and significant kings of the Chola Empire Sir. So, I would want to understand the vision behind the establishment of massive Shiva temples like the Brihadisvara Temple or Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Where did that vision and planning come from? How did the thought occur to them to create something that would inspire people for the next one or two thousand years? So, that is what I would like to know from them. And, the second personality – who, in my opinion, is a highly underrated personality in Indian history – Sir, his name is Hemu. We usually read only two or three lines about him in Indian history.

Krishna Seshadri: We often don’t know the fact that Hemu was a common man – an ordinary individual and a merchant – who went on to build an empire; he was not just an empire-builder but also a military thinker and a military genius who fought 23 battles in his career and won 22 of them. I am very interested in understanding his thought process and the journey that took him from being an ordinary man to such a great king, Sir. The third figure is a very interesting personality – a woman named Tribhuvan Mahadevi. Her story belongs to the Bhaumakara dynasty of Odisha. Around 850 AD, the neighbouring Pala Empire invaded her kingdom, and her husband – the king – was martyred in the battle. Consequently, the empire shrank, and chieftains and leaders began abandoning it; however, Tribhuvan Mahadevi took charge of the administration. She became one of the first independent rulers in Indian history. She not only stabilized the government but also made it powerful enough to rule over Kalinga and the surrounding region for the next hundred years. So, these are the three interesting historical personalities I would like to meet, Sir.

Prime Minister: Krishna-ji, it seems like you are re-living history now; you’ve been completely immersed in it. See, I have also viewed your site with great interest, and what I found most fascinating was the tab allowing people to submit corrections and suggestions. Being open to such constructive feedback is a significant thing in itself.

Have you started receiving suggestions from people? And how do you act upon them?

Krishna Seshadri: Yes, Sir, we receive many suggestions from people. Suggestions generally fall into two categories. One type involves suggesting corrections – such as pointing out which king ruled a specific region or nation at a particular time, or clarifying when a specific battle took place. We receive other suggestions – such as adding specific features to the website – and we consider them all. For instance, if someone suggests that a particular king ruled a specific region during a certain era, we take that suggestion and cross-reference it with our sources. Someone suggested to us that while we had showcased India as a whole, it would be even better to display information similarly at the regional level; so, we implemented that feature. And then another suggestion led us to create a ‘trump card’ style feature – compiling data and statistics for various empires – to make the content more engaging for children. Someone also suggested consolidating these resources so they could be easily downloaded and shared, a feature we are currently implementing. It’s important for us to know that we are bound to make mistakes – we aren’t the best. That is precisely why we consciously included a ‘correction’ tab; we want this to be a collaborative platform where contributions help us build a site that makes history an enjoyable subject for years to come.

Prime Minister: Krishna-ji, you have truly accomplished something remarkable. Okay, apart from history, you must be having a lot of other hobbies… or do you engage in other activities as well!

Krishna Seshadri: Well, actually, Sir, I’m a bit of a boring person.

Prime Minister: (Laughs)

Krishna Seshadri: I’m deeply interested in technology and history, and now that the two have come together, I spend my entire day immersed in that.

Prime Minister: Well, Krishna ji, I extend my very best wishes to you. You have made a good start, and your approach is such that people will connect with it – I am fully confident of that. My best wishes are with you.

Friends,

This initiative by Krishna ji will help not only history students but all of us to learn about our past in an engaging way. If you also have information about such initiatives, please do share it.

My dear countrymen,

The ‘Nasha-mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat’ campaign is currently gaining momentum rapidly across the country. Its goal is absolutely clear: drug-free youth; a drug-free India.

I am happy that this campaign has not remained merely a formality; many people – especially our youth – are becoming a part of it in large numbers. After all, this is our collective resolve for the health, happiness, and bright future of India’s youth.

Friends,

Drug addiction does not just engulf a single individual; the entire family and society have to bear the consequences. I would like to commend those who raise awareness against drugs and step forward to help individuals struggling with addiction. Can you come up with a powerful slogan for a drug-free India? Can our young musicians create songs that convey the message of a drug-free life? Can students and theatre groups write touching short plays that highlight the dangers of drugs while also showing the path to recovery? Our country has no shortage of excellent content creators. I urge them to create content in various languages ​​that helps society in this endeavor. You can use your creativity as a medium for social change. Do share your efforts on social media using the relevant hashtag. Often, creative efforts prove more impactful than formal campaigns. Let us all play our part in this noble mission to keep India’s youth away from drugs and free from addiction. Do share your efforts on social media with the hashtag #NashaMuktYuva

My dear countrymen,

The month of August brings with it myriad hues of patriotism all around. During this time, the spirit of love for the nation intensifies in everyone’s heart. Occasions such as ‘National Handloom Day’ and the anniversary of the ‘Quit India Movement’ to ‘Partition Horrors Remembrance Day’ make this month special. ‘Independence Day’ and ‘National Space Day’ fill every countryman with pride. The ‘Har Ghar Tiranga’ campaign further strengthens this sentiment. This year has become even more special as it marks the 150th anniversary of ‘Vande Mataram’. This time, over 8 crore ‘Tiranga selfies’ were uploaded.

And this celebration of the Tricolour was not limited to India alone; this year, through the ‘Suryapath Tiranga’ initiative, our flag embarked on a unique journey across the globe. The Tricolour was hoisted in Suva, Fiji, at the first light of dawn. Subsequently, it was unfurled at Indian Missions and Posts across Asia, Africa, Europe, and eventually San Francisco in America. You can imagine how magnificent those scenes must have been; as the sun traversed across the world, the Indian Tricolour was hoisted in its wake. Such efforts bind society together and deepen our connection with the nation. I extend my heartiest congratulations to everyone involved in these initiatives.

My dear countrymen,

From morning till evening, lakhs of women across the streets of our cities and towns are engaged in their work. Some sell vegetables or fruits, others run tea stalls, while some sell flowers, earthen lamps, and worship materials. Often, a mere lack of capital prevents their businesses from growing further. But now, lakhs of such mothers and sisters are gaining new strength through the ‘PM SVANidhi Yojana’. This aspect of ‘women empowerment’ is not discussed as much as it should be. Women account for approximately 46 percent of the beneficiaries of the ‘PM SVANidhi Yojana’. This means that around 35 lakh women across the country are expanding their businesses by connecting with this scheme.

Friends,

Babita Sharma ji from Ghaziabad is an excellent example of this.
